I likewise, valorous <term>Madonna</term> <note>A formal title of respect for a high-born woman, equivalent to "My Lady."</note>, judge that what can be done by those who have known the loftiness of your soul is fittingly dedicated to you, and that their beautiful thoughts, nourished by your divine spirit, must turn back to you; and in honor of your name, they should strive as much as they can, seeing that they learn true virtues no less from the example of your life than those ancient philosophers did from the columns of Mercury. # DIALOGUE

<note>Space at the start of the first line suggests a missing ornamental initial B.</note> considers it well that others should live; and those who, mired in earthly things, cannot suddenly rise to this celestial thought, provided they turn their eyes toward you—illuminated by your radiance—are purified little by little, and make themselves worthy of the high <term>contemplation</term> <note>In this context, contemplation refers to the Neoplatonic practice of rising from the observation of physical beauty to the understanding of divine truth.</note> of your divinity. Therefore, recognizing this common debt, as well as my own, I have done as those who, unable to pay from their own resources, pay with the wealth of others. Desiring to discharge part of this great obligation I have toward you, and being unable—due to the poverty of my own wit—to send you fruit born of myself, I send it to you grown in the gardens of another: namely, the books of love by **Master Leone** <note>Leone Ebreo (c. 1460–1535), also known as Judah Leon Abravanel, was a Jewish philosopher and physician whose "Dialogues of Love" became one of the most influential works of the Renaissance.</note>, under the names of **Philo** and **Sophia** <note>The names of the two characters in the dialogue; Philo represents "Love" or "Lover" and Sophia represents "Wisdom" in Greek.</note>. This is a chaste subject of love for a chaste lady who breathes love; celestial thoughts for a lady adorned with celestial virtues; and the highest understandings for a lady filled with the highest concepts. Thus, I preferred to show you my desire to satisfy my debt through the work of another, rather than prolong my obligation because of my own poverty.

Though I believe (when I think on it) that I am making two significant gains at once: settling part of my debt to you, and making **Master Leone** my debtor (if shadows <note>The author refers to the deceased Leone Ebreo as a "shadow" or spirit.</note> can be beholden). For I have drawn these divine dialogues of his out of the darkness in which they lay buried and placed them, as it were, into clear light. By recommending them to the name of such a valorous lady as you are, I am certain he must greatly rejoice; both for this new splendor and for such high protection, he must remain much obliged to me. You, therefore, having become the guardian of this work, by directing your radiance toward it—as toward a body most fit to receive light—will cause it to appear more splendid and more miraculous to the world.

# THE FIRST DIALOGUE ON LOVE,
## BY LEONE EBREO <note>original: "Leone Hebreo". Leone Ebreo (c. 1460–1535), born Judah Leon Abravanel, was a Jewish physician and philosopher. This work, "Dialoghi d'amore", became one of the most widely read books of the 16th century.</note>
### THE SPEAKERS.
-> <term>PHILO</term> AND <term>SOPHIA</term>. <-
<note>The names are symbolic: Philo represents "Love" or "the Lover" (from the Greek *philos*), while Sophia represents "Wisdom" (from the Greek *sophia*). Together, they personify "Philosophy"—the love of wisdom.</note>
-> PHILO. <-

<image-desc>Large woodcut historiated initial 'I' within a square frame, depicting a man standing in a hilly landscape with trees.</image-desc>THE knowing of you, O Sophia, causes both love and desire within me. *SO. These affections that the knowledge of me produces in you seem discordant to me, O Philo; but perhaps your passion makes you speak so.* *FI. They discord only with yours, which are far from any reciprocation.* SO. Rather, even between themselves, to love and to desire are contrary affections of the will. *FI. And why contrary?* SO. Because, regarding those things we judge to be good: we love those which we have and possess; and those which we lack, we desire. In such a way, that which is loved is first desired; and after the desired thing is obtained, love arrives and desire fails. FI. What moves you to hold this opinion? SO. The example of things that are loved and desired. Do you not see that when we do not have health, we desire it? But we would not yet say we love it. And once we have it, we love it, and we do not desire it. Riches, inheritances, and jewels: before they are possessed, they are desired and not loved; after they are obtained, they are no longer desired, but loved. FI. Although health and riches cannot be loved when they are missing (because we do not have them), nonetheless, they are loved "to be had" <note>Philo is arguing that we "love the idea" of possessing these things even when we lack them.</note>. SO. This is an improper way of speaking: saying "to love" when you mean "to want"

<summary>The dialogue begins with Philo confessing his love and desire for Sophia, leading to a philosophical debate on the definitions of love versus desire. Sophia argues that they are mutually exclusive, as desire is for what we lack and love is for what we possess.</summary>
<keywords>Philo, Sophia, love vs desire, Neoplatonism, definition of love, possession, health and wealth</keywords>

It does not seem possible for love and desire to coexist. **FI.** Your arguments, O Sophia, show the subtlety of your wit more than the truth of your opinion. For if we do not love that which we desire, we would be desiring something we do not love—and consequently, something that is abhorred and hated. He who has none cannot love them, but he desires them; and he who has them does not desire them, but loves them. **FI.** Just as you demonstrate with the example of children, you ought to remember the husband: who, before he is won, is both desired and loved at the same time; and after he is won, desire fades, and sometimes love as well—though in many cases it not only perseveres but even grows. The same often happens to the husband regarding the wife. --- Page 11 ---
<meta>This page continues the philosophical investigation into the relationship between love and desire. Sophia has just argued that love concerns things that exist, while desire concerns things that do not yet exist or are not possessed. Philo now probes the logical consequences of this distinction regarding the role of knowledge.</meta>

->F I R S T<-

**PHILO.** For what reason does love presuppose the existence of things?

**SOPHIA.** Because it is necessary that knowledge precede love: for nothing could be loved if it were not first known under the appearance of goodness; and nothing falls within our knowledge if it is not first actually found in existence: because our mind is a mirror and a pattern—or to put it better, an image of real things—so that there is nothing that can be loved before it is found to actually exist. <note>In Renaissance philosophy, the mind was often described as a "speculum" (mirror) that reflects the external world. Sophia argues that for the mind to "reflect" a thing as good, that thing must first exist in reality.</note>

**PHILO.** You speak the truth: but for this very same reason, desire can only apply to things that have existence: because we only desire those things that we first know under the appearance of goodness; and for this reason the philosopher <note>original: "il filosofo". This refers to Aristotle, who famously begins the *Nicomachean Ethics* by stating that "the good" is "that at which all things aim" or desire.</note> has defined the good as that which everyone desires, since knowledge is of things that exist.

**SOPHIA.** It cannot be denied that knowledge precedes desire: but rather I would say that not only is all knowledge of things that are, but also of those that are not: because our intellect <term>intelletto: the capacity for rational thought and understanding</term> judges a thing that exists as it is, and likewise judges another that does not exist. Since its office is to discern between the being of things and their non-being, it must know both those that are and those that are not. I would say, then, that love presupposes the knowledge of things that are, and desire the knowledge of things that are not, and of those things of which we are deprived.

**PHILO.** For love as much as for desire, knowledge of the thing loved or desired as good precedes the feeling; and for neither of them should the knowledge be of anything other than the good: because such knowledge would be the cause of making one totally abhor the thing known, and not desire it,

<summary>Philo and Sophia debate whether knowledge—which must precede both love and desire—requires the object to actually exist, concluding that love is for existing things while desire is for things known but not yet possessed.</summary>
<keywords>Aristotle, Being vs. Non-Being, Theory of Knowledge, The Good, Nature of Desire, Intellect</keywords>

<meta>This page continues the debate between Philo and Sophia regarding the nature of love and desire. Philo has just argued that knowledge—and thus the perceived existence of a thing—must precede both love and desire. Sophia is now challenging this by pointing out that we often desire things that turn out to be false or non-existent.</meta>

-> D I A L O G O <-
<meta>catchword: this</meta>

...to praise it, or love it; so that love, just like desire, equally presuppose the being <note>original: "l'essere". In this context, it refers to the ontological status or existence of an object.</note> of things, both in reality and in knowledge. **SO.** If desire presupposed the being of things, it would follow that whenever we judge a thing to be good and desirable, such a judgment would always be true: but do you not see that it is many times false, and the thing is not found to be so in its actual being? It would seem, then, that desire does not always presuppose the being of the desired thing. **FI.** This very same defect of which you speak occurs no less in love than in desire: because many times that thing which is esteemed good and lovable is actually bad and ought to be abhorred; and just as the truth of the judgment of things causes right and honest desires, from which derive all virtues, temperate acts, and laudable works; so the falsehood of such judgment is the cause of evil desires and dishonest loves, from which all human vices and errors derive: such that the one, just like the other, presuppose the being of the thing <note>Philo argues that even if a judgment is wrong, the mind treats the object as having a certain "being" or quality (goodness) before the emotion of love or desire is triggered.</note>. **SO.** I cannot fly so high with you, O Philo; let us come, please, a bit lower. I still see that none of those things which we most desire exist in a way that they can properly be loved. **FI.** We do indeed always desire that which we do not have, but not for that reason do we desire that which does not exist: rather, desire is usually for things that exist but which we cannot possess. **SO.** Yet it is also usually for those things that effectively are not <note>original: "non sono". Sophia refers to events or states of being that haven't happened yet.</note>, and we desire indeed that they might come to be, though we do not desire to "possess" them in a physical sense: such as when we desire that it rain, when it is not raining; or that there be good weather, or that a friend should arrive, or that something should be done: which things, because they are not, we desire that they might be, in order to benefit from them, but not to possess them; nor for this...

<summary>Sophia and Philo debate whether desire requires the object to exist; Philo argues that both love and desire stem from our mental judgment of a thing's "being," while Sophia notes we often desire non-existent events like rain.</summary>

--- Page 13 ---
<meta>This page continues the dialogue between Sophia and Philo. Sophia has just suggested that we desire things that do not exist. Philo is now responding by refining the definitions of "being" and "nothingness," arguing that even desired things possess a form of "possible being" that precedes the emotion of love or desire.</meta>

# FIRST BOOK #

<meta>catchword: the acquisition</meta>

*...this, we shall say we love them: so that desire is indeed for things that are not. **PH.** That which has no being at all is nothing; and what is nothing, just as it cannot be loved, so too can it not be desired or possessed. And these things you mentioned—though they do not exist in a state of present actual being <note>original: "essere attuale". The state of existing in reality right now, as opposed to potentially.</note> when they are desired—nonetheless, their being is possible <note>original: "essere possibile". Potential existence; something that could exist but does not yet.</note>. And from that possible being, one can still desire that they come into actual being; just as with those things that already exist but which we do not have: from the perspective of their existence, we can desire that they be possessed by us. So, all desire is either for that which is not yet to come into being, or to possess that which we lack. How do you want it then? Does not every desire presuppose being in part, and privation <note>original: "privatione". A technical term in Aristotelian philosophy meaning the absence or lack of a quality that a thing should naturally possess.</note> in part, and does it not desire the fulfillment that it lacks in its being? Thus, desire and love are founded on the being of the thing, and not on its non-being. Furthermore, for a desirable thing, three "titles" or attributes must precede it in order: the first is being; the second is truth; and the third is that it be good. With these, it comes to be loved and desired. This could not happen if it were not first esteemed as good; for otherwise it would not be loved or desired. And before it is judged good, it must be known as true; and since it must really exist before it can be known, it must have real being. For first the thing exists in being, then it is imprinted upon the intellect <note>The faculty of the mind that understands and thinks.</note>, then it is judged to be good, and finally it is loved and desired. And for this reason the Philosopher <note>A common title for Aristotle (384–322 BCE), whose theories on logic and metaphysics dominated Renaissance thought.</note> says that being, truth, and goodness are interchangeable <note>original: "si convertono in uno". Referring to the doctrine of the "transcendentals," where Being, Truth, and Goodness are seen as different ways of describing the same fundamental reality.</note>; except that being is the thing in itself; truth is when the thing is imprinted on the intellect; and goodness is when it moves from the intellect and the will toward the acquisition...*

<summary>Philo argues that love and desire are rooted in the existence (being) of an object, categorizing existence into "actual" and "possible" states. ...of three kinds: useful, delightful, and virtuous <note>original: "honeſte". In this context, it refers to moral goodness or things sought for their own sake, following the Aristotelian tradition.</note>; these relate differently to love and to desire.

**PH[ILO].** It is not as easy as you might think to define love and desire with a definition suited to all their species, for their nature is found differently in each of them; nor do we read that the ancient philosophers gave them such a broad definition. Nevertheless, for what suits our present discussion, I define desire as a voluntary affection <note>original: "affetto uolontario". A movement of the will toward an object.</note> for the being or the having of a thing esteemed as good which is lacking; and I define love as a voluntary affection to enjoy, through union, the thing esteemed as good. From these definitions, you will not only recognize the difference between these effects of the will—that one, as I told you, is to enjoy the thing through union, and the other is for its being or its possession—but you will also see through them that desire is for things that are lacking. However, love can be for things that we possess, and also for those we do not possess; because the impulse to enjoy through union can be a voluntary affection both for things we lack and for things we have. For such an affection does not presuppose either possession or lack; rather, it is common to both.

**SO[PHIA].** Even though these definitions might require a more extensive explanation, they are sufficient for me as an introduction to what I ask you concerning the cause of the diversity found in loving and desiring across the three kinds you mentioned: the useful, the delightful, and the virtuous.

In those honorable things, the more excellent the love and desire, the more worthy the virtue and honor. However, the useful and the pleasant can only possess intellectual reason through the moderation and the **middle path** <note>original: *mediocrità*; in the Aristotelian sense of the "Golden Mean," a balance between two extremes</note> of the love and desire for them. For such loves, when stripped of reason, are bad and vicious, and belong more to brute animals than to men. The middle path that reason creates in this context is the only true love. And from that middle path, it is proven that the more excessively it is desired, loved, and followed, the more truly it is virtue; because such a desire is no longer mere pleasure or utility, but depends on the moderation of those things, which is an intellectual virtue and truly an honorable thing.

# FIRST DIALOGUE

...ary, <note>completing the word *honorario* from the previous page</note> honor, fame, and glory, which are all things that are loved and desired. For while on one hand they seem pleasant because of the delight achieved in possessing them, on the other hand, it seems they are not; because once they are possessed and held, they are still loved without reaching a state of satiety or disgust <note>original: *fastidio*; the Renaissance concept that physical pleasures eventually become tiresome or repulsive once satisfied</note>—a quality that would seem to belong more to useful and honorable things than to pleasant ones.

<margin>PHILO</margin> Health, even though it achieves utility, has the pleasant as its own proper quality. It is not inconsistent for some pleasant things to be useful, just as many useful things are pleasant; and in both categories, some are found to be honorable. Health, then, primarily possesses a delight suited to its nature. It is not only useful, but also honorable, and for this reason, being "full" of it is not tedious, nor does it ever become a burden like other purely pleasant things—which, when possessed, are not valued as much as when they are missing and desired. There is yet another reason why one does not grow weary of health or find it tiresome: because the sensation of its delight is not located only within the external material senses—such as taste in the case of food, or touch like carnal pleasure, or smell like perfumes, which quickly become wearisome—but it is also present within the spiritual senses, which are more slowly satisfied. For it does not consist only in hearing, like sweet harmonies and soft voices, nor even in seeing, like beautiful and well-proportioned figures; rather, the delight of health is felt with the entirety of human sensation, both the external and internal senses, and even...

<meta>This page continues the dialogue between Sophia (Wisdom) and Philo (Love). Philo is explaining that God is the ultimate end of all things. The conversation here pivots to an epistemological challenge: how can a finite human mind know or love an infinite God? Philo uses sensory metaphors to explain that knowledge is limited by the capacity of the knower, not the object being known.</meta>

### DIALOGUE ###

->D I A L O G O<-

...of God must exceed every other honorable love and virtuous act.

**SO.** I have heard you say before that because He is infinite and in all perfection, He cannot be known by the human mind, which is in every way finite and limited. For that which is known must be comprehended <note>In this philosophical context, "comprehend" means to fully grasp or "contain" the entirety of a concept within the mind.</note>; and how shall the infinite be comprehended by the finite, or the immense by the small? And if He cannot be known, how can He be loved? For you have said that a good thing must first be known before it can be loved.

**FI.** The immense God is loved only as much as He is known. And just as He cannot be entirely known by men, nor can His wisdom be fully grasped by the human race, so He cannot be entirely loved by men to the degree that He deserves. Nor is our will capable of such excessive love. However, it is the duty of our mind to know according to its own possibility of knowing, but not according to the immense excellence of the thing known. Nor does our will love Him according to what He is worthy of being loved, but only as much as our will can extend itself toward Him in the act of loving <term>atto amatorio: the active expression of love or the state of being in love</term>.

**SO.** Can a thing be known if it is not comprehended by the one who knows it?

**FI.** It is enough that one comprehends that part of the thing which is known; the known is comprehended by the knower according to the power of the knower, and not according to the power of the thing known. Do you not see that the form of a man is imprinted and comprehended in a mirror, not according to the perfect human being <note>original: "perfetto eſſere humano," referring to the actual physical and spiritual existence of a person</note>, but according to the capacity and strength of the mirror's perfection—which is only figurative and not essential? Fire is comprehended by the eye not according to its burning nature (for if it were so, it would burn the eye), but only according to its color and shape. And what greater example...

<summary>Philo addresses the paradox of how finite humans can love an infinite God, explaining that we know and love God according to our own limited capacity, much like a mirror reflects an image without becoming the object itself.</summary>

# THE FIRST.

...example: that the great hemisphere <note>The "hemisphere" refers to the visible dome of the sky or the celestial vault.</note> of the sky is encompassed by so small a part as the eye? See how great its smallness is, for some wise men are found who believe it to be indivisible, unable to receive any natural division. Therefore the eye comprehends things according to its own ocular power, its size, and its nature, but not according to the condition of the things seen in themselves. And in this same way our small intellect <term>intellect (intelletto): in Renaissance philosophy, the faculty of the soul that perceives universal truths</term> comprehends the infinite God, according to human capacity and intelligible power, but not according to the bottomless ocean of the divine essence and immense wisdom. To this knowledge, the love of God serves and responds in accordance with the ability of the human will, but not in proportion to the infinite goodness of that most perfect God.

**SO.** Tell me, is desire mixed into this love of God?

**FI.** On the contrary, divine love is never stripped of ardent desire, which is to acquire what is lacking in divine knowledge. In such a way, as knowledge grows, the love of the known divinity grows as well; for the divine essence exceeds human knowledge in infinite proportion, and His goodness no less exceeds the love that humans bear for Him. Therefore, there always remains for the happy man a most ardent and unrestrained desire to continually increase his knowledge and divine love. Man always has the possibility of this growth from the side of the object known and loved; although on his own part, it could be that such effects are determined at a level beyond which man cannot reach further, or perhaps even after reaching the highest degree, an impression of desire remains in him to know what he lacks without ever being able to attain it, even though he were blessed <note>original: "beato"—referring to the state of "beatitude" or ultimate spiritual happiness in the presence of God</note>,

<meta>This page continues the philosophical dialogue between Sophia and Philo regarding the nature of human knowledge and the love of God. On the previous page, Philo explained that although the human mind is small compared to God’s infinity, it can still know and love Him according to its own capacity. He concluded by mentioning that man always has the possibility of attaining a blessed state.</meta>

-> D I A L O G U E <-

...blessed state, because through the excellence of the soul, God is an object placed above human power and habit <term>habit (habito): a settled disposition or acquired tendency of the mind, such as a virtue or a skill</term>. Although such remaining desire in the blessed should not cause suffering due to lack—since it is not a human impossibility to have more—it rather gives them the highest delight to have reached the extreme limit of their own possibility, both in the knowledge and the love of the divine.

**SO.** Since we have come to this point, I would like to know in what manner this human beatitude <term>beatitude (beatitudine): supreme blessedness or the highest state of happiness</term> consists.

**FI.** The opinions of men regarding the subject of happiness have been diverse. Many have placed it in utility, in the possession of the goods of fortune <note>In Renaissance philosophy, "goods of fortune" referred to external things like wealth, power, and status, which are subject to luck rather than one’s own character.</note>, and the abundance of such things for as long as life lasts. But the falsity of this opinion is manifest: because such exterior goods are caused by interior ones, in such a way that the former depend on the latter. Happiness must consist in the most excellent things, and this happiness is the end <note>The "end" or "final cause" refers to the ultimate goal or purpose for which a thing exists.</note> of all other things, and does not exist for any other purpose, but rather all things exist for it. This is especially true since such exterior goods are in the power of fortune, whereas happiness must be in the power of man. Some others have held a different opinion, saying that beatitude consists in the pleasurable: and these are the Epicureans <note>Followers of the ancient Greek philosopher Epicurus; in the Renaissance, they were often (sometimes unfairly) characterized as prioritizing physical pleasure above all else.</note>, who maintain the mortality of the soul and believe nothing in man to be happy except for delight in whatever manner. But the falsity of their opinion is not hidden either: because the pleasurable corrupts itself when it reaches satiety and disgust, while happiness gives entire contentment and perfect satisfaction. Furthermore, we said above that the end of pleasure is the honorable <term>honorable (honesto): the morally good or virtuous, sought for its own sake rather than for profit or pleasure</term>, and happiness is not for any other end; rather, it is the final cause of every other thing. So, without doubt, happiness consists in honorable things.

### F I R S T  B O O K

...noble things, and in the acts and habits of the intellectual soul <term>intellectual soul (anima intellettiua): in the philosophy of the time, this refers to the highest part of the human soul responsible for reasoning and understanding, which distinguishes humans from animals</term>, which are the most excellent and the ultimate goal of all other human habits. These are the means by which man is truly man, possessing more excellence than any other animal.

**SO.** How many, and of what kind, are these habits of intellectual acts?

**FI.** I say that there are five: **Art, Prudence, Intellect, Science, and Wisdom.**

**FI.** *Art is the habit of things to be made according to reason; these are things made with the hands and through physical labor. # FIRST.

(as Aristotle <note>Aristotle (384–322 BCE), the Greek philosopher whose theories on the soul and the "agent intellect" were central to medieval and Renaissance thought</note> says) the nature of our intellect is capable of understanding and receiving everything, just like the nature of the agent intellect <term>agent intellect (intelletto agente): in Aristotelian philosophy, the active power of the mind that makes knowledge possible by "illuminating" abstract ideas</term>, which is that which creates intellectual likenesses and illuminates our intellect with them, making you perform every intellectual act, and illuminating and imprinting every thing upon the possible intellect <term>possible intellect (intelletto possibile): the human capacity to receive knowledge, which starts as a "blank slate" or potentiality</term>; and this is nothing other than being led from its dark potentiality to the illuminated act through the agent intellect. 

It follows, then, that its ultimate perfection and its happiness must consist in being entirely transformed from potentiality into the act of all things that have being; because since the intellect is in potentiality to all things, its perfection and happiness must lie in knowing them all, in such a way that no potentiality or deficiency remains in it. And this is the ultimate bliss and happy end of the human intellect. In this state, they say that our intellect is entirely deprived of potentiality and is made actual, and in all things it unites and converts itself into its illuminated agent intellect, through the removal of potentiality (which is the cause of its diversity). In this way, the possible intellect becomes pure in act, and this union is the ultimate perfection and true bliss; and this is called the happy conjunction <term>conjunction (copulatione): the high-level intellectual or mystical union where the human mind and the universal intellect become one</term> of the possible intellect with the agent intellect.

**fi.** Why? 

**so.** Because if a man cannot be blessed until he has known all things, he will never be so: for it is almost impossible for a man to come to the knowledge of all things that exist, due to the brevity of human life and the diversity of things in the universe.

This doctrine alone deals with spiritual and eternal things. Since it is necessary first to know Him and then to love Him, it follows that happiness consists not in knowledge, but in the love of God, which is the final act.

<meta>This page continues the philosophical investigation into the nature of ultimate happiness, known as beatitude. Filone is detailing the two schools of thought: those who believe happiness is an act of the "will" (loving and enjoying God) and those who believe it is an act of the "intellect" (knowing and perceiving God). This mirrors the classic debates between Franciscan and Dominican scholastic traditions.</meta>

->D I A L O G U E<-
<meta>catchword: forward</meta>

They also find support in the notion of delight, which is central to happiness and belongs to the will. Whence they say that the true happy act is voluntary—that is, love—in which delight consists, and not in the intellectual act, because it does not participate in delight in the same way. Others, on the contrary, make this argument: they say that happiness consists in the act of the most principal and spiritual power of our soul. Since the intellectual power is more fundamental than the will and more abstracted from matter, it follows that **beatitude** <term>beatitude (*beatitudine*): the state of supreme, eternal happiness or "blessedness" achieved through union with the Divine.</term> does not consist in the act of the will (which is to love Him); rather, they say that love and delight follow from knowledge as accessories, but are not the primary end.

<meta>This page continues Filone’s explanation of the five senses. In the previous section, he argued that while the higher senses (sight, hearing, smell) are insatiable and lead to greater wisdom, the lower senses (taste and touch) are prone to satiety and loathing. ->F I R S T<-

...these two <note>Referring to the senses of taste and touch mentioned at the end of the previous page.</note> more than any of the other senses, which are seeing, hearing, and smelling. The reason for this is that these three are not necessary for the individual existence of man, nor even for the successive existence <term>successive being: the survival of the human race through reproduction</term> of the species; rather, they exist solely for the convenience and benefit of men and perfect animals <note>In the Aristotelian tradition, "perfect animals" are those that possess all five senses and the ability to move, as opposed to "imperfect" creatures like shellfish.</note>. Therefore, just as their existence is not strictly necessary for survival, they have no need for boundaries or limitations in their operation. And just as not seeing, not hearing, or not smelling does not deprive a man of his life, neither is his life taken away by superfluous seeing, superfluous hearing, or frequent smelling—unless it should happen by accident. 

But taste and touch are different; just as their existence is necessary for human life and the continuation of the species—so much so that if they did not exist, life would be lost—so too their excess would cause the destruction of man. For eating and drinking too much would kill a man no less than hunger and thirst. Likewise, frequent carnal union <note>original: "copula carnale"</note> and excessive heat or cold in the sense of touch would cause his corruption. Since there is a bond of greater delight in these two senses due to their necessity for the personal and successive being of man, it is necessary to limit them naturally. For even if delight should transport them toward a harmful excess, a natural limit should restrain them, so that such excess cannot destroy the individual. 

In this way, nature has shown no less wisdom in placing a natural limit and a brake upon the senses of taste and touch for their own preservation than she did in producing them for man's existence. And although the appetite of the lover is satiated through the union of copulation, and that desire—or rather, appetite—continually ceases, it is not for this...

<summary>Filone explains that the senses of taste and touch are governed by natural limits and satiety because they are essential for survival and reproduction, whereas the higher senses like sight and hearing are unlimited as they serve human convenience rather than basic biological necessity.</summary>

And because love, once it is born, is deprived of all <term>reason: "ragione," the logical and discerning faculty of the mind</term>, it is depicted as blind, without eyes. And because his mother, Venus, has beautiful eyes, she therefore desires the beautiful; and reason judges the person to be beautiful, good, and lovable: and from this, love is born.

Cupid is also depicted as naked, because a great love cannot be hidden with reason nor covered with <term>prudence: "prudenza," the ability to govern oneself with caution and foresight</term> because of the unbearable pains he inflicts. And he is a small child because he lacks prudence, nor can he be governed by it. He has wings because love enters the soul with speed, and with speed it makes the soul go out to always find the beloved person, abstracted from itself; for this reason, Euripides <note>The Greek playwright; this specific quote refers to a common ancient sentiment that the soul of the lover dwells in the body of the beloved</note> says that the lover lives in the body of another.

He is depicted shooting arrows because he wounds from afar, and he shoots the heart as his specific target. Furthermore, the wound of love is like that of an arrow: sudden, narrow at the opening, and of deep penetration; it is not easy to be seen, difficult to treat, and very grave to heal. To one looking from the outside, it seems like little, but in its inner nature it is most dangerous, and most of the time it turns into an incurable <term>fistola: a deep, narrow, and persistent ulcer or sore</term>. And further, just as the wound made by an arrow is not healed even if the bow is snapped or the string that shot it is broken, so that which true love inflicts is not remedied by any delight that fortune might grant, nor by anything the beloved person might give at any time; nor can the wound be closed even by the loss of the beloved in irreparable death. So, do not wonder if perfect love, being the son of reason, is not <note>The text cuts off here; the catchword indicates the next word is "ordered" or "governed."</note>

<summary>Filone explains the classical imagery of Cupid—his blindness, nudity, childhood, wings, and arrows—as allegories for the irrational, persistent, and painful nature of deep intellectual love. He argues that while love is born from a rational recognition of beauty, it quickly escapes the control of reason.</summary>

Who can deny that in honest loves one finds marvelous and unrestrained desires? What is more honest than <term>divine love: "amor diuino," the love of God</term>? It is certainly not governed by the reason that rules and preserves man; for many, out of divine love, do not value their own person and seek to lose their life. Some, out of their great love for God, "un-love" themselves, just as the unhappy, through loving themselves too much, "un-love" God. And coming to the conclusion, how many have sought to end their lives and consume their persons, inflamed by the love of virtue and <term>glorious fame: "gloriosa fama," the pursuit of a lasting legacy</term>? Ordinary reason does not allow such things; rather, it directs everything so that one may live honorably. I would tell you also that many have sought to die cheerfully for the love of their honest friends—of whom I could give you many examples, but I leave them out so as not to be tedious. Furthermore, I do not think that inflamed love and the unrestrained affection of a man for a woman is any less irreproachable than that of a man for a man, provided it is born...

It makes a man entirely alienated from himself and belonging to the person he loves. In fact, it considers anyone who gives advice or help to be a mortal enemy. ...so many things, O Filone, that I see clearly that in lovers the tongue is more abundant than the passion. **FI.** It is a sign that you do not feel these passions, because you do not believe them; for no one can believe the magnitude of a lover's pain except the one who shares in it. My <term>spirits: "spiriti," the vital vapors thought to carry life and sensation through the body</term> burn, my heart is consumed, and my whole person is a conflagration. One who finds himself in such a state: if he were able, do you not believe he would free himself? But he cannot, because he has no liberty to free himself, nor even to seek to be freed. How then can one be governed by the reason of one who is not in his own liberty? For all physical subjections leave only the will free, but the subjection of love is that which first seizes the <term>will: "volontà," the faculty of choice and intention</term> of the lover, and after that, the entire person together. **SO.** There is no doubt that lovers suffer many afflictions until they have achieved what they most desire, but afterward...

...all the storm turns into a calm, so that these pains proceed more from the desire for the thing not yet possessed than from the actual love of it. **FI.** In this, too, you do not speak as one with experience; for those lovers whose pains cease with the achievement of carnal delight, their love does not depend on reason, but on carnal appetite, and (as I have told you before) their pains and passions are carnal, not spiritual. They are unlike those immense pains of wondrous <term>penetration: "penetratione," the philosophical concept of two souls or spirits intermingling or occupying the same spiritual space</term> and intolerable stinging felt by those lovers whose love depends on reason. Such people receive no remedy for their grief nor mitigation of their love through carnal delight; on the contrary, I tell you and affirm that if their pains were great before, after such a union they are much greater and more unbearable. **SO.** What is the cause, that having what they desire, their passion should increase? **FI.** Because such love is a desire for the perfect union of the lover with the beloved person, which cannot be achieved except through the total penetration of the one into the other. This is possible in souls, which are spiritual, because incorporeal spirits can, through mental and highly effective powers, interpenetrate, unite, and be <term>converted: "conuertirsi," the process of the soul transforming its essence into that of the beloved</term> into one. But in distinct bodies, each of which requires its own specific place, such union and penetration—relative to what is desired—remains incomplete. This leaves behind a desire even more burning for that union which cannot be perfectly achieved; and as the mind always seeks the total conversion into the beloved person, it abandons its own self, existing always with greater affection and pain because of the failure of that union, which

<note>Filone is articulating a core Neoplatonic paradox: because human beings are both soul and body, the soul's desire for perfect, spiritual oneness is frustrated by the physical reality of separate bodies that cannot occupy the same space.</note>

<meta>catchword: natural,</meta>

...which neither reason, nor will, nor prudence can limit, nor resist. **SO.** It seems to me that my mind somewhat yields to your arguments; but one thing alone remains strange for me to concede: that love, or any other good thing, could be found in man, or in the world, that is not governed by reason—since it is manifest that she is the regulator and governor of every good and laudable thing, and a thing is worthy only when it participates in reason. How, then, can you affirm that perfect love is not governed by her? **FI.** Since this alone remains a doubt for you, I wish to clarify this one point in our present <term>discussion: "confabulatione," a formal philosophical dialogue or conference</term>. You should know that in men, two kinds of reason are found. One we shall call <term>ordinary reason: "ragione ordinaria," the practical logic used for self-preservation and social conduct</term>, and the other extraordinary. The intent of the first is to rule and preserve man in an honest life, whereby all other things are directed toward this end; and everything that impedes a good human life, reason turns away from and reproves. This is that reason which I told you cannot regulate or limit perfect love: because such love prejudices and harms one's own person, life, and well-being with intolerable damage in order to follow the beloved person. But the intent of <term>extraordinary reason: "ragione straordinaria," a higher, ecstatic logic that prioritizes the beloved over the self</term> is to obtain the beloved thing. It does not attend to the preservation of one’s own interests; rather, it sets them aside to acquire the thing that is loved, just as one must set aside the less noble for the more excellent. For, as <note>Filone refers to Aristotle, commonly called "The Philosopher" in medieval and Renaissance texts.</note> the philosopher says, the beloved has the status of being more perfect than the lover: because being the "end" or goal of the lover, the end is more noble than that which exists for the sake of the end. Therefore, it is reasonable to exert oneself for that which is greater. And you can understand this by example...

<summary>Filone distinguishes between "ordinary reason," which focuses on self-preservation and morality, and "extraordinary reason," which compels a lover to sacrifice their own well-being for the beloved, whom they view as a more noble "end" than themselves.</summary>

-># DIALOGUE<-

<meta>catchword: oneself,</meta>

self, both natural and mortal. Naturally, you will see someone struck in the head, and they will instinctively put their arm forward to save the head because it is more noble <note>In Renaissance philosophy, "noble" refers to a thing's rank in the hierarchy of being; the head is "nobler" than the arm because it houses the senses and reason</note>. Thus, the lover and the beloved having been made one, and the beloved being the more noble part of this union, while the lover is the less noble, naturally the lover does not shun any affliction or pain to acquire the beloved. With every care and diligence, the lover follows the beloved as their true goal, abandoning everything belonging to themselves as if it were something belonging to another. 

The moral example is this: just as <term>ordinary reason: "prima ragione," the basic logic of self-interest</term> commands us to preserve wealth for our own needs so that we may live well and comfortably, the <term>extraordinary reason: "seconda ragione," the higher logic of virtue</term> commands us to distribute it appropriately to others for a more noble end, which is to acquire the virtue of <term>liberality: "liberalità," the classical virtue of generous giving</term>. Therefore, the first reason commands us to seek utility and honest pleasures, but the second commands us to weary and trouble the mind and the person for a more noble cause, one that is rightfully worthy of being loved.

**SO.** Which of these two kinds of reason do you think, Filone, ought to be followed?

**FI.** The second is more worthy and of a more eminent degree, just as the <term>prudence: "prudenza," practical wisdom or foresight</term> of the generous man is more sublime in dispensing wealth virtuously than the prudence of the miser in accumulating it for his own needs. For while it is indeed prudence to acquire wealth, it is greater and more worthy to distribute it liberally. A man who, through reason, preserves a worthy and excellent love within himself without ever enjoying it is like a tree that is always green, large, and abundant in branches, but bears no fruit; such a tree can truly be called sterile. And without doubt, few virtues accompany the person who lacks excellent love. It is certainly true that he who diverts oneself—

GOD save you, O Filone. Do you pass by like this without speaking? **FI.** She who is the enemy of my health greets me; yet God save you, O Sofia. What do you want from me? **SO.** I would like you to remember the debt in which you are bound to me. -># D I A L O G O<-

*...is not only in these; rather, its commonality extends to many more things in the world.* **SO.** Tell me first, what other causes of love are found in living beings; and then you will tell me how love can also be found in inanimate and non-generative <note>Objects that do not reproduce, such as stones or elements.</note> things. **FI.** I will tell you the one, and then the other. Animals—besides naturally loving things that are suitable for them to seek, just as they hate unsuitable things to flee from—also love each other reciprocally for five reasons: first, for the desire and the delight of generation <note>Procreation.</note>, as males with females; second, for generative succession, as fathers and mothers with their children; third, for benefit, which not only generates love in the receiver toward the giver, but no less causes it in the giver toward the receiver, even if they were of different species; for it is seen that if a bitch or a goat <note>original: "cagna, ouero una capra"</note> nourishes a child, they have for one another a very great love, and so it is if one nourishes some other animal of a foreign species; fourth, for the commonality of the same species, or another very similar, for you will see individuals of every species of non-predatory animals keep company because of the love they have for one another; even the predators, although they do not keep company so as to enjoy the whole hunt alone, nonetheless have respect and love for those of their own species, so as not to use against them their natural and cruel ferocity or venomousness; and furthermore, among different species of animals, some friendly similarity is found, such as the Dolphin with man, just as others are found who hate each other naturally, such as the Basilisk <note>A mythical reptile said to kill with its gaze; here used as a real example of natural antipathy.</note> and man, who kill each other with sight alone; fifth, through continuous companionship, which

...which not only makes animals of one and the same species friends, but also those of different species and hostile natures—as one sees a Dog with a Lion, and a Lamb with a Wolf, becoming friends through companionship. **SO.** I have understood the cause of love among animals; tell me now those of the love of men. **FI.** The causes of reciprocal love among men are these same five found in animals, but the use of reason makes them more intense or more relaxed, either directly or indirectly, according to the diversity of the human end <note>The "end" refers to the ultimate goal or purpose of human action.</note>. **SO.** Explain these differences to me in each of these five causes. **FI.** The first—desire and the delight found in generation <note>Procreation.</note>—is in men a cause of more intense, firm, and exclusive love than in animals, but it is usually more concealed by reason. **SO.** Explain these differences more specifically. **FI.** It is more intense in men because they love women with greater vehemence; they seek them with such great solicitude that for them they leave off eating and sleeping and postpone all rest. **FI.** Knowledge, and appetite, and consequently love, exist in three modes: natural, sensitive, and rational-voluntary.

**SO.** Explain all three to me.

**FI.** Natural knowledge, or appetite, or love, is that which is found in non-sensing bodies, such as the elements <note>The four classical elements: Earth, Water, Air, and Fire</note> and those bodies composed of the inanimate elements, such as metals, and types of stones, and even plants, herbs, or trees. This inclination moves them toward that end, just as **heavy bodies** <note>In the Aristotelian physics of the time, "heavy" objects like earth and water naturally moved toward the center of the universe</note> are moved to descend below, and **light bodies** to ascend above, as if to a place they know and desire. These inclinations I call—and they truly are—natural appetite and love.

Sensitive knowledge and appetite, or love, is that which is found in irrational animals. They use it to pursue what is beneficial for them <note>original: "il loro conueniente"</note> and flee what is harmful, such as seeking food, drink, the proper temperature <note>original: "temperie"</note>, mating, rest, and similar things. It is necessary to first know these things, and then desire or love them, and thereafter pursue them. For if the animal did not know them, it would not desire them nor love them; and if it did not desire them, it would not pursue them in order to have them; and not having them—

**SO.** Tell them to me at length.

**FI.** I will begin with the last, which is the love of the same species <note>original: "amor della medesima specie." In Aristotelian and Neoplatonic physics, things of the same kind have a natural affinity to be near one another.</note>, because it is more manifest. You will see that the parts of earth that find themselves outside the whole move with effective love to unite with all the earth; and thus the stones that congeal in the air <note>Likely referring to hail or perhaps meteorites, which were thought to form in the upper atmosphere and then fall to their "natural home" on Earth.</note> quickly seek the earth. And the airy vapors, or winds, that are generated in the concavity of the earth, strive to exit with earthquakes, desiring to find their element of air because of the love they have for their species. And so fire, which is generated down here, moves to ascend to the place of its element in the upper region for the love of its species.

**SO.** I understand the love that the elements have for their own species; tell me of the other causes.

**FI.** I will speak of the penultimate of the five causes of love, which is the fourth: the love of society <note>original: "società." Here meaning association or partnership between different elements.</note>, because it too is manifest, being proportioned to natural places.

**SO.** And what other society is found in the elements and in such bodies?

**FI.** Each of the four elements—that is, earth, water, air, and fire—enjoys rest near certain others, and not near the rest. The earth flees the proximity of the heavens and of fire, and seeks the center <note>In the geocentric model, the Earth is at the absolute center of the universe, the point furthest from the celestial spheres.</note>, which is the furthest point from the heavens; and it likes to be near the water and near the air when it is below it, but not when it is above; for finding air above it, the earth flees to the depths, and never rests until it is distanced from the heavens as much as possible.

**SO.** And why does it do so, since from heaven comes every good?

**FI.** [Earth] does so because it is the heaviest <note>original: "grave." In Renaissance physics, gravity was the tendency of "heavy" elements to move toward the center of the universe.</note> and thickest of all the elements, and being sluggish, it enjoys rest more than any of the others. Since the heavens are always in continuous motion without ever resting, the earth, in order to remain quiet, moves as far from them as it can. Only in the center—which is the lowest point—does it find rest, surrounded by water on one side and by air on the other.

**SO.** I have understood regarding the earth; tell me of the water.

**FI.** Water also possesses something of the heavy and the sluggish, but less so than the earth and more so than the others. For this reason, it also flees from the heavens so as not to move with such velocity as the air and fire do. It seeks the low places and likes to stay near the earth—but above it—and below the air. It feels love for these, but toward fire it feels enmity and hatred; it flees from fire and distances itself from it, for it cannot endure to be with fire without the company of the others <note>This refers to the idea that fire and water are "contraries" (hot/dry vs. cold/moist) and require a mediating element like air or earth to coexist in a compound.</note>.

**SO.** Tell me of the air.

**FI.** Because of its lightness and <term>subtlety</term> <note>original: "sottilità." This refers to a substance being thin, fine, or ethereal, the opposite of "gross" or "dense."</note>, the air enjoys the celestial nature and proximity. It seeks the heavens with lightness as much as it can and ascends to the heights—though not immediately next to the heavens, because it is not of a substance as purified as fire, which takes the first place. Therefore, the air loves to be near the fire, situated beneath it; it also loves the proximity of water and earth, but it cannot suffer being below them, only above. With ease, it follows the continuous <term>circular motion</term> <note>The "moto circulare" refers to the belief that the upper atmosphere is pulled along by the rotating celestial spheres.</note> of the heavens. It is friendly toward both fire and water; and because these two are contraries and enemies to one another, the air has placed itself between them as a friend to both, so that they cannot destroy each other with continuous war.

**SO.** It remains to know of the fire.

Therefore, not only in the Latin language does "man" <note>original: *homo*</note> signify both the male and the female, but also in the most ancient Hebrew tongue—the mother and origin of all languages—"Adam," which means "man," signifies both male and female, and in its proper meaning encompasses both together. Pythagoras proposed that within it there were a right and a left side, just as in every other perfect animal; he said that the majesty of heaven from the equinoctial line <term>equinoctial line: the celestial equator</term> up to the arctic pole, which we call the North <note>original: *tramontana*</note>, was the right side of heaven. This was because, from the equator toward the North, he saw fixed stars that were larger, clearer, and greater in number than those he saw from the equator toward the other pole. It also seemed to him that heaven caused a greater and more excellent "generation" <note>The creation or bringing-forth of life and matter</note> in the lower things of that part of the earth than in the other. He calls the other half of heaven—stretching from the equinoctial line to the other antarctic pole, which we cannot see—the left side of heaven. But the philosopher Aristotle, confirming that heaven is a perfect animal, says that it not only has these two parts of an animal (that is, right and left), but that it possesses the other parts of a perfect animal in addition to these,

### SECOND.

...perfect; that is to say, front and back (which are the face and shoulders) and up and down (which are the head and feet). In a living animal, all these six parts are found to be distinct and different. Furthermore, the "right" and the "left" presuppose the other four parts, for without them they could not exist. This is because the right and the left are parts of the *width* of the animal's body, while up and down—that is, the head and the feet—are parts of the *length*, which naturally precedes width. The front and the back—that is, the face and shoulders—are parts of the *depth* of the animal's body, which is the foundation of both length and width. Thus, if there are a right and a left in the heavens, as Pythagoras says, it follows that the other four parts belonging to the other two dimensions must also be found there: the head and feet from the dimension of length, and the face and shoulders from the dimension of depth.

*Aristotle* says that our pole <note>The North Pole</note> is not the right side of heaven, nor is the other pole the left, as Pythagoras claimed. He argues this because such a difference—and the superiority of one over the other—would not exist within the heavens themselves, but only in how they appear to us or in relation to our position. It may be that in the other part of the world unknown to us, there are more fixed stars in the sky and more habitations on the earth. In our own times, the experience of the navigations of the Portuguese and the Spaniards <note>A reference to the Age of Discovery and the exploration of the Southern Hemisphere</note> has demonstrated part of this to us.

Therefore, Aristotle says that the East is the right side of heaven and the West is the left. He proposes that the entire body of heaven is an animal, the head of which is the Antarctic pole <note>The South Pole</note>, which is hidden from us, and the feet are the Arctic pole toward the North <note>original: *tramontana*</note>. In this way, the "right" remains in the East and the "left" in the West. The face is that part which moves from East to West, and the shoulders, or the back—

...back, and that part which is from the west to the east below. So that the whole universe being a man, or rather an animal that contains both male and female, and the heaven being one of the two perfectly with all its parts, you can certainly believe that the male is the man, and that the earth and the **prime matter** <term>materia prima: the fundamental, formless substance that underlies all physical reality and takes on various forms</term> with the elements is the female; and that these two are always joined in matrimonial love, or in the reciprocal affection of two true lovers, as I have told you.

**SO.** I like what you have told me of Aristotle concerning the **animality of the heaven** <note>The classical and Renaissance idea that the cosmos is a living, ensouled organism rather than a mechanical system</note>, and of its six parts which are naturally distinct in an animal. Even in plants, although a difference between head and feet is found—in that the head is the root and the feet are the leaves—so that a plant is an animal in reverse, oriented from top to bottom, yet the differences of the other parts are not found in them, for they have neither face, nor shoulders, nor right, nor left side. 

But regarding this point where Aristotle says that the East is the right side of heaven and the West is the left, a doubt occurs to me: that East and West are not the same for all inhabitants of the earth. On the contrary, our East is the West to others who live below us, who are called the **Antipodes** <note>From the Greek, meaning "those with feet opposite to ours"; a term used for people living on the opposite side of the globe</note>; and our West is East to them. Indeed, all parts of the curvature of the heaven from the rising to the setting sun are East to certain inhabitants of the earth and West to certain others. Which of these Easts, then, shall be the right side, and why one more than another? And if every East is the right side, then one and the same place would be both right and left. Resolve this for me, for it seems doubtful.

**FI.** Your doubt, O Sophia, is not very easy to resolve. Some say that the East which is the right side of heaven is the East of those who inhabit the middle of the length of the world’s habitation,

**SO.** This is true.
**FI.** Not at all, for it is not true: because we know that the greater part of the earth’s roundness from the east to the west is exposed, and that every place has its own sunrise <note>original: "oriente"</note>, and one should not be considered the "right" more than another—especially since what is east to one person is west to another. **SO.** For what reason?
**FI.** Because when the Sun is in ***Aries***, it possesses great power, and at that time all plants are born and the world grows young again; and when it is in ***Libra***, they all go about drying up and growing old.
**SO.** Even if it were so, ***Aries*** would not be the right side for that reason, since it is not always in the east, but sometimes in the west; and when it is east to one, it is west to another: and **Aristotle** <note>The author refers to Aristotle’s *On the Heavens*, where the philosopher attempts to assign anatomical directions to the cosmos</note> declares that the east is the right.
**FI.** You prove it well, especially since the Sun is not so benevolent or such a benefactor to all inhabitants of the earth when it is found in ***Aries***: because those on the other half of the earth who live beyond the **equinoctial** <term>equinottiale: the equator</term> and see the other **antarctic pole**, who are called ***Antichthones*** <term>Antitoni: a Greek term for people living on the opposite side of the globe whose seasons are reversed</term>, receive the benefit of spring when the Sun is in ***Libra***, because it then begins to approach them. And they experience the decline of autumn when it is in ***Aries***, for then it moves away from them, contrary to us. Therefore, our right would be their left; and yet the right side of an animal is the right for everyone, and likewise the left.

The other three parts are the opposites of these in such operations.

Following this path of motion, it is always the "right" and never the "left"; for the sky never moves, nor does any of its parts, in a direction contrary to that right-handed motion. For this reason, the motion of the planets is "left-handed," moving in reverse to act against the right-handed celestial motion. They do this to favor the lower opposites and to allow for their continuous <term>generation: the process of birth and the creation of new life, typically paired with "corruption" or decay</term>.* 

**SO.** *I have understood you, and I am satisfied regarding my doubt. These are found in him not only as distinct powers and operations, but are even divided among the members, parts, and locations of the human body.* 

**SO.** *Teach them all to me.*

...of all three specifically. **FI.** The human body is divided into three parts, following the pattern of the world, stacked one above the other. *   Hot, dry, and thin **choler** <note>original: "collera"; also known as yellow bile</note>, which has the quality of fire; 
*   Hot and moist **blood**, gently tempered, which has the quality of air; 
*   Cold and moist **phlegm**, which has the quality of water; 
*   And the cold and dry **melancholic humor**, which has the quality of earth. 

Furthermore, just as animals are generated from the four elements (which, beyond nutrition and growth, possess sensation and motion), as well as plants (which have no sensation or motion, but only nutrition and growth), and other mixed things devoid of a soul—lacking sensation, motion, nutrition, and growth, being like the dregs of the elements, such as stones, <gloss>fuochi: flints or mineral sparks</gloss>, salts, and metals—so too from these four humors generated in this first and lowest section, members are generated that possess nutrition, growth, sensation, and motion, such as the nerves, membranes, tendons, and muscles; and others are formed that lack sensation or motion of their own, such as the bones, cartilage, and veins. This is what corresponds in man to the Divine Principle, from which all things have their beginning, and toward which all things are directed and find rest, as their ultimate end.

### SECOND [DIALOGUE]

->H 3<-

Pythagoras used to say that the celestial bodies, in moving, generated excellent voices, corresponding to one another in harmonic concordance. This <term>celestial music: also known as the "Music of the Spheres," the ancient idea that the movement of stars and planets creates a divine harmony</term>, he said, was the cause of the sustenance of the entire universe in its weight, in its number, and in its measure. He assigned to every sphere and to every planet its own sound and voice, and he declared the harmony resulting from them all. And he said the reason why this celestial music is not heard or perceived by us is the distance of the heavens from us, or rather our habituation to it, which causes it not to be felt by us—just as happens to those who live near the sea, who do not hear its noise because they are used to it, unlike those who approach the sea for the first time. 

Since, therefore, love and friendship are the cause of all concordance, and since in the celestial bodies there is a greater concordance—firmer and more perfect than in all the <term>inferior bodies: the physical things on Earth made of the four elements</term>—it follows that between them there is a greater and more perfect love, and more...

# S E C O N D O.
## H 4

*...low <note>original: "graue," referring to low-pitched musical notes</note>, a whole song is generated, sweet to the ear, and if one of these is missing, the entire song or harmony is corrupted. Likewise, from these bodies differing in size and in low and high <note>original: "lieue," literally light, here referring to the fast or high-pitched motion of the spheres</note> motion, there is composed from them—by their proportion or conformity—a **harmonic proportion** so great and so unified that if the smallest particle were missing, the whole would be undone. Thus, this natural conformity is the cause of love among the celestial bodies, not only as distinct persons, but as members of a single person. For just as the heart loves the brain and the other members, and provides them with life, natural heat, and spirits; and the brain provides the others with nerves, sense, and motion; and the liver provides blood and veins, because of the love they have for one another, and because each loves the whole as its own part—a love which exceeds any love for any other person—so too the parts of heaven love one another reciprocally with natural conformity. And by all concurring in a union of purpose and action, they serve one another and provide for each other's needs, in such a way that they form a perfectly organized celestial body. Furthermore, there is in them that other cause proper to the love of men, which is **virtue**: for since every one of the celestial bodies possesses an excellent <term>virtue: an inherent power or specific quality that allows a being to perform its cosmic function</term>, which is necessary for the existence of the others and of the entire heaven and the universe, once such virtue is known by the others, they love those others for it. And I will also say that they love them for the benefit they perform—not a specific or individual benefit toward one, but a universal benefit throughout the entire universe, for without that, everything would be destroyed. First of all, they establish the literal sense—like an outer **rind**—which is the history of certain people and their notable, memorable deeds. Then, within that same framework, they place the moral sense like an inner rind closer to the **marrow** <note>original: "midolla," referring to the core or pith of a plant/fruit, used here as a metaphor for the deeper truth within a story</note>. Sometimes two, or even all three of these <term>scientific senses: higher levels of interpretation that explain the laws of nature, the stars, or divine reality</term> are included within the fable, like the marrow of the fruit within its rinds.

This is a "natural" allegory because man is part of the natural world. 

It also intends to signify another **celestial allegory**: that celestial nature, the daughter of Jove, having caused mortality and corruption in bodies through its continuous motion...

Furthermore, for even greater preservation, they have expressed history in **weighty verses** <note>Refers to poetry with strict meter and rhythm.</note> that are most carefully observed, so that they cannot easily be corrupted. [He] <note>The context suggests Philo is referring to Plato, who transitioned from the traditional poetic verse of the ancients to philosophical prose while retaining the "lock" of allegorical myths.</note> removed one lock from that knowledge—the lock of verse—but he did not remove the other, that of the fable <note term="fable">In this context, "fable" (fabula) refers to myths or allegorical stories used to hide deeper philosophical or theological truths.</note>. He broke the law of preservation entirely and spoke of the matters of philosophy in a scientific style in prose <note term="scientific style">A systematic, literal, and demonstrative way of writing, as opposed to the allegorical or mythological style of earlier thinkers.</note>. 

It is quite true, however, that he employed such marvelous artifice by being so brief, so comprehensive, and so full of profound meaning, that this sufficed for the preservation of the sciences in place of verse and fable. This was so much the case that when he replied to his disciple Alexander of Macedon <note>Alexander the Great.</note>—who had written to him expressing surprise that he had made public the secret books of sacred philosophy—Aristotle replied that his books were published and not published <note>original: "editi, et non editi"</note>, for they were published only to those who had understood them from his own mouth. ### SECOND ###

I

...of which <note>The text likely refers to the Platonists or Plato himself, continuing from the previous page.</note> they have their own specific natures, which he calls Ideas; he holds that the Idea of fire is true fire by its formal essence, and the elemental fire we see is fire only through its participation in that Idea, and so it is with the others. It is not, therefore, strange to attribute divinity to the Ideas of things. For this reason, they also placed divinity in plants—most especially in those that are the most common and useful foods for humans, such as Ceres for the grains and Bacchus for wine—because of the universal utility and necessity that men have for them. For plants, too, have their own Ideas just as the elements do. By this same reasoning, they also called the virtues, the vices, and human passions gods and goddesses. Because, beyond the fact that the virtues (due to their excellence) and the passions (due to their force) participate somewhat in divinity, the principal cause is that every one of the virtues, every one of the vices, and every one of the human passions has its own universal Idea. Through participation <note term="participation">In Platonic philosophy, 'participation' (methexis) is the relationship between individual, physical things and the eternal, perfect 'Ideas' or 'Forms' they reflect. A beautiful object 'participates' in the Idea of Beauty.</note> in these Ideas, these traits are found in men more or less intensely or mildly. For this reason, among the gods are named Fame, Love, Grace, Greed, Pleasure, Strife, Toil, Envy, Fraud, Stubbornness, Misery, and many others of this sort; for each has its own Idea and incorporeal principle, as I have told you, by which it is named a god or goddess.

...Saturn, and Mars, from whom every evil derives: so also among the Platonic Ideas there are some principles of good, and of virtue, and others that are principles of evil, and of vices. **SOPHIA.** How then does it not decay and perish, as lower bodies do?

**PHILO.** Plato says that the heavens are corruptible by their own nature, but divine power makes them indissoluble. He refers to the intellectual forms <note>Non-material archetypes or divine ideas that give structure to matter.</note> in action that shape them. Furthermore, because these celestial elements are purer—acting almost as the "souls" of the lower elements—they are not mixed together in heaven as they are in the lower world. Fire exists only in the luminous parts, and water only in the transparent parts. Thus, although Strife, at the beginning of the production from the womb of Chaos, wished to ascend to heaven, it was nonetheless cast into the lower world, where its habitation remains today. # DIALOGUE

**So.** Why do they attribute all these children to Erebus and to Night?

**Ph.** Because they all derive from inherent potential <note>original: "potentia inherẽte"; the capacity for change or becoming within matter.</note> and from nocturnal privations, both in the great world below <note>the macrocosm or the physical universe.</note> and in the small human world <note>the microcosm.</note>.

**So.** Tell me how.

**Ph.** Love—that is, desire—is generated by inherent potential and by lack: because matter, as the philosopher <note>referring to Aristotle, who famously wrote that matter "desires" form as a female desires a male.</note> says, desires all those forms of which it is deprived. Grace is that quality of the desired or loved thing which persists in the desiring mind, or in the appetitive power. Toil represents the anxieties and labors of the desirer to reach the thing they crave. Envy is what the desirer feels toward the one who possesses. Fear is the dread of losing what has been newly acquired—since everything acquired can be lost—or of being unable to acquire what one desires. Deceit and fraud are the means of acquiring desired things. Persistence is what one uses in pursuing them. Want, misery, and hunger are the deficiencies of those who desire. Complaint is their lament when they cannot have what they desire, or when they lose what they have acquired. Disease, old age, and words <note>original: "parole"; likely referring to the fading or "passing" of things through time/speech.</note> are the dispositions toward the loss and corruption of things acquired through will or the power of generation. Darkness and sleep are the first admissions <note>or "preludes."</note>, while death is the final corruption. Charon is the oblivion that follows the corruption and loss of what was acquired. Day <note>original: "Die"; from the Latin *Dies*.</note> is the luminous form which inherent material potential—that is, the human intellectual power—can reach; and in man, it is the shining virtue and wisdom toward which the will and desire of the perfected person are directed. Aether <note>original: "Ether"; the fifth element or the substance of the heavens.</note> is the celestial intellectual spirit,

**Ph.** Because many of the ancients, and Plato along with them, affirm that these celestial natures are made from the matter of lower bodies <note>this refers to the philosophical debate over whether the heavens are made of a unique "fifth element" or a refined version of common matter.</note>; hence they turn out to be the most excellent children of Erebus.

**So.** What you have briefly said regarding the generation of Demogorgon <note>a primordial deity in Renaissance mythology, often seen as the father of all gods and the personification of the creative power of nature.</note> is sufficient for me. I only lack an understanding of things pertaining to love, such as the falling in love of Pan—the second son of Demogorgon—with the nymph Syrinx.

**Ph.** The poets depict the god Pan with two horns on his head reaching toward the sky, a fiery face with a long beard hanging over his chest. He holds a staff in his hand and a flute with seven pipes <note>original: "fistula cõ sette calami"; the syrinx or pan-pipes.</note>. He wears a skin spotted with various markings, has lower limbs that are rough and coarse, and goat-like feet. They say that when Pan came into conflict with Cupid <note>original: "Cupidine"; the god of love.</note> and was defeated by him, he was forced to love Syrinx, a virgin nymph of Arcadia. While Pan pursued her and she fled, she was blocked by the river Ladon; when she asked the other nymphs for help, she was transformed into reeds, or marsh canes. The hair and the long beard hanging over his chest are the rays of the Sun and other planets and stars, which hang down into the lower world to bring about every generation and mixture of matter. Among these members, the feet are goat-like because goats' feet never walk in a straight path, but go jumping and traversing in disorder; such are the feet of the lower world, and its movements and transformations from one essence into another transversally, without a certain order—roughness and disorder from which the celestial bodies are free.
