### SECOND BOOK

furthermore, this universal nature—so great, powerful, excellent, and admirable—cannot be without love. Therefore, it loved the pure and uncorrupted virgin; that is, the stable and incorruptible order of worldly things. Nature loves what is best and most perfect, but while nature followed this order, the order fled from it, because the lower world is so unstable and always inordinately changeable, moving with goat-like feet <note>A reference to the previous page, where Pan's goat feet symbolize the rough, erratic movements of the elemental world</note>. 

The flight of this virgin brought her to the river Ladon—that is, the heavens, which run continually like a river. Within these heavens is held that uncorrupted, fleeting stability of the generable bodies <term>generable bodies: physical things in our world that are born, change, and eventually perish</term> of the lower world. Although the heavens are not without their own continuous instability due to their constant local motion, this instability is ordered and eternal: a virgin without corruption. Its apparent irregularities exist with an ordered and harmonious correspondence, just as we spoke above concerning celestial music and melody. 

These are the reeds of the river-canes into which Syrinx was transformed; in these reeds, the spirit generates a sweet sound and harmony, because the intellectual spirit that moves the heavens causes their consonant musical correspondence. From these reeds, Pan made the flute <note>original: "fistola"</note> using seven of them, which signifies the gathering of the orbs of the seven planets <note>In the ancient world, these were the Sun, Moon, Mercury, Venus, Mars, Jupiter, and Saturn</note> and their wonderful harmonic concords. For this reason, it is said that Pan carries a staff and the flute upon which he always plays, because nature continually makes use of the ordered movement of the seven planets to guide the constant changes of the lower world. 

You see, O Sofia, how briefly I have explained the substance of Pan’s love for Syrinx. 

**SO.** I enjoy this account of Pan’s falling in love with Syrinx. Now I would like to know about lineages, marriages, and adulteries.

The allegory of this is quite manifest: for the Heaven, which surrounds, conceals, and covers all things, is the son of Ether and Day, because it is composed of an ethereal nature in its subtle and spiritual transparency, and of a divine luminous nature through the bright stars it possesses. Ether is called the "father" for being the principal part of heaven, both for its greatness that encompasses all the spheres <note>original: "orbi"</note>, as well as—according to **Plotinus**, following the mind of **Plato**—because it penetrates the entire universe, which he posits as being full of ethereal spirit. 

He argues that the luminous bodies are particular members of heaven in the manner of the woman, who is part of the man, who is the whole <note>An analogy suggesting that the stars are dependent parts of the greater unified "body" of the heavens</note>; and also because ether is a thinner and more spiritual body than the luminous bodies of the stars and planets. Hence **Aristotle** says that, because the stars are of a thicker and denser corporeality than the rest of the Heaven, they are capable of receiving and retaining light within themselves—which the celestial sphere cannot do because of its transparent thinness. **Fi.** <note>Filone</note> I understand her as the governing power <term>governing power: the inherent "virtue" or force that directs natural processes</term> of the lower world and of all the elements, and most especially of the air, which is that which surrounds and encompasses the water, and which penetrates the earth everywhere. Hence, because of the universality of air throughout the globe, which is most appropriately attributed to Juno, she is the governing power of the whole sublunar world, of generation, and of the elements, just as Jove <note>Jupiter</note> is the governing power of the celestial bodies.

And since they are contiguous with one another, they are called siblings.

This is according to what Anaxagoras <note>A Pre-Socratic Greek philosopher</note> says, which conforms with Holy Scripture regarding the production, or creation, of the world, when it says that from a single principle and seed of things, God created the heaven and the earth. Finally, they appeared on the Island of Delos—which represents the first uncovering of the earth (which in the beginning was not large), situated like an island within the waters. They appeared there both because of the receding of the water and because the air in that place was not so thick. 

For this reason, in the sacred account of creation, it is told that after the things created on the first day, the night and the day were [ordered]; on the second day, the ethereal firmament was stretched out, which was the division of the air, the water, and the earth. Afterward, on the third day, the earth itself was uncovered, giving a beginning to the production of plants; and on the fourth day occurred the appearance of the Sun and the Moon above...

Thus, he sometimes gives a love that is neat, pure, clear, manifest, and sweet, according to his own proper Jovial nature.

...influences in her not only great beauty, but also burning lust, according to her nature of causing in the lower world a delightful life and concupiscible generation <note>“Concupiscible generation” refers to the drive toward reproduction motivated by physical desire.</note>. This is because Mercury is mutable by nature, taking on the qualities of the planet with which he blends: when mixing with a masculine planet, he is male, and with a feminine one, he is female.

Among men, many were called "Mercuries," especially certain Egyptian sages and physicians who shared these "Mercurial" virtues. Because Mercury is a bright planet, they call him the son of **Heaven** <note>original: "Cielo," referring to Uranus</note> and **Day** <note>original: "Die," the goddess of the day</note>, because he shares celestial substance with the light of day—for the light of all planets comes from the **Sun**, which creates the day. He is the brother of **Venus** because the planets are related, and these two planets are joined; each of them completes its orbit in nearly the same time—that is, in one year—and they always travel near the **Sun** without distancing themselves too far from him. For this reason, they are said to be siblings. Others consider **Mercury** the son of **Jupiter** because of his divine wisdom and power, and say he was nursed by **Juno**, because human wisdom proceeds from divinity and is sustained by material writings, which are signified by **Juno** <note>Juno here represents the physical or material medium of knowledge, such as books or scrolls.</note>. <meta>This page continues Philo’s explanation of the mythological figures Mercury and Apollo as allegories for human faculties and social roles. It picks up mid-sentence from the previous page, discussing how "Mercurial" individuals (those defined by intellect and eloquence) interact with "Solar" individuals (those defined by power and authority).</meta>

->D I A L O G O<-

<meta>catchword: chart [tà]</meta>

thefts to acquire, through deceit and in secret, the abundance and wealth of Kings and great masters; this is because they are often administrators and royal secretaries due to their **Mercurial** aptitude. This is what it means when it is said that Mercury stole the cattle from Apollo: for Apollo signifies and creates powerful lords, and the cattle are their riches and abundance. And when these princes are angry with them for their thefts, they free themselves from that anger through **Mercurial** cunning, by removing the causes from which punishment might come to them, and by mitigating the fury of the lords, they remain in their favor. Furthermore, Mercury's low status <note>Referring to Mercury's position as the planet closest to the sun and often "hidden" by its light</note> ensures they are not harmed by the fury of great masters, because they offer no resistance; for just as Mercury is the smallest of all the planets, the solar rays and their **combustion** <term>combustion: an astrological condition where a planet is so close to the Sun that its effects are said to be "burned up" or hidden</term> harm him less than any other planet when they are joined together.

Mercury gives Apollo the lyre <note>original: "cethara"</note>, and Apollo gives him the rod. This means that the **Mercurial** wise man serves the prince with harmonious prudence and sweet eloquence (signified by the lyre); and the prince lends the **Mercurial** wise man power and authority, giving credit and reputation to his wisdom. Thus Plato says that power and wisdom ought to embrace one another, because wisdom tempers power, and power favors wisdom. It also signifies that when the Sun and Mercury are brought into perfect conjunction in a favorable place in the **birth chart** <term>natività: a horoscope or astrological map of one's birth</term> and in a good zodiac sign, they cause the **Mercurial** man of letters to be powerful, and the **Solar** man and great master to be wise, prudent, and eloquent.

**SO.** You have told me enough about the **birth chart**.

*...[by] his light, sensible things are seen and discerned, from which knowledge and wisdom derive. And since this bow is generated by the radiation of the Sun’s circumference into the thick and humid clouds, and the difference in their thickness causes the diversity of its colors—according to the varying way the clouds receive the light—it follows that the Sun's bow is that which, by God’s command, creates the stability and the security that there shall be no more floods.

**SO.** In what way does the Sun, with his bow, give us such security?

**FI.** The Sun does not leave its mark when it makes the bow in thin and clear air, but only in thick and humid air. If this air were of a density sufficient to cause a flood through a multitude of rains, it would not be capable of receiving the impression of the Sun and forming the bow; therefore, the appearance of this impression and bow assures us that the clouds lack the density to create a flood. This is the stability and the security that the bow provides regarding the flood, the cause of which is the power of the Sun, which purifies the clouds in such a way and thins them so that, by imprinting its circumference upon them, it makes them incapable of producing a flood. Wherefore, with reason and wisdom, they have said that *Apollo* killed *Python* <note>original: "Fitone"; the serpent Python represents the stagnant, rotting moisture left after a flood</note> with his bow and his arrows; for which deed, although *Apollo* was proud and haughty according to the solar nature <note>The "solar nature" refers to the Sun's dominant, high-reaching, and life-giving position in the heavens</note>, yet he could not free

It could be said that the purpose of such exhalation was the nourishment of the heavenly beings; for poets hold that they feed on the vapors that ascend from the humidity of the globe of the earth. 

But since this is still metaphorical, it is understood that the Sun and the planets are maintained primarily in their own office—which is to govern and sustain the lower world, and consequently the whole of the universe—through the exhalation of humid vapors. Therefore, he [the Sun] loves humidity to convert it to himself for his needs, but she [the humidity] flees from the Sun, because everything flees from that which consumes it. Furthermore, the solar rays cause humidity to penetrate through the vapors of the earth and make it flee from the surface; and thus the Sun dissolves it. When it is already inside the earth and cannot flee further from the Sun, it is converted into trees and plants, with the help and influence of the celestial gods who generate all things, and with the help of the rivers that restore it and aid it against the persecution and grasp of the Sun. All of these have a sextile aspect of sixty degrees' distance and are feminine, sharing the same active quality—namely, they are cold—even though they differ in their passive quality from dry to moist, just as earth differs from water. Therefore, their friendship is partial and imperfect.

**FI.** Because one is for the purpose of receiving, and the other is for giving. **FI.** Your doubts are of considerable importance. The solution to the first is that in the order of the universe, the inferior depends upon the superior, and the corporeal world upon the spiritual. Thus, a lack in the inferior would bring a lack to the superior upon which it depends, because the imperfection of the effect denotes an imperfection in the cause. Therefore, when the cause loves its effect, and the superior loves the inferior, it desires the perfection of that inferior and desires to unite with it to free it from defect; for by freeing the inferior, the superior saves itself from lack and imperfection. So it is that when the inferior does not come to unite with the superior, not only does the inferior remain defective and unhappy, but the superior also remains stained by a lack of its own sublime perfection—just as a father cannot be a happy father if his son is imperfect. And he says that such a goal is more noble and more excellent than the mover itself, because the goal of a thing is more noble than the thing itself. Of the four causes of natural things—which are the material, the formal, the agent cause (which makes or moves the thing), and the final cause (which is the goal that moves the agent to act)—out of all of them, the material is the lowest. The formal cause is better than the material, and the agent is better and more noble than both because it is the cause of them. But the final cause <term>final cause: the "telos" or ultimate purpose of an action, which motivates the entire process</term> is the most noble and excellent of all four—more even than the agent cause, because the agent is moved to act for the sake of the goal. Thus, the goal is called the "cause of all causes." Because such souls are separate from matter, and since its sphere is the one that contains and embraces the entire universe and moves all the other heavens with its own movement, that intelligence which informs, moves, and gives it being must be the supreme God, and nothing else. For by being a mover, He does not make Himself equal to the others; rather, He remains much higher and more sublime, just as His sphere is more sublime than those of the other intelligences. And just as His heaven comprises and contains all the others, so His power contains the power of all the other movers. If, by being called a mover like the others, He were equal to them, then according to the first group <note>the thinkers who double the number of intelligences</note>, He would also be equal to the other final intelligences <note>final intelligences: spiritual beings acting as the "goal" or purpose of a sphere's movement</note>, by being, like them, the goal of the first mover. In conclusion, *Averroes* <note>original: "Auerrois"; a major medieval commentator on Aristotle</note> says that to posit more intelligences than those which the force of philosophical reason induces is not the mark of a philosopher, since otherwise one cannot see except as far as reason demonstrates to us.

**SO.** This opinion seems more limited to me than that of the first group. But what will he say regarding what *Aristotle* <note>original: "Ariftotele"</note> affirms—and reason with him—that the goal <note>term: "fine" (end/goal). In Aristotelian thought, the "end" or purpose of a thing is always superior to the thing itself</note> of the sphere's mover is more excellent than the mover itself?

**FI.** *Averroes* says that *Aristotle* means that the same intelligence that moves is also its own end <note>original: "fine"</note> in its continuous movement. This is because it moves the sphere to fulfill its own perfection, according to which it is more noble for being the goal of the motion than for being the efficient cause <note>term: "efficiente" (efficient cause). The agent that actually produces the motion, as opposed to the "final cause" which is the purpose for which it moves</note> of it. Therefore, this saying of *Aristotle* is instead a comparison between the two types of causality <note>original: "caufalità"</note> that are found within one and the same intelligence...

<summary>Filone explains Averroes' view that the highest heaven is moved by God Himself, who acts as both the mover and the goal. He argues that Aristotle's distinction between a mover and its goal is actually a comparison of functions within a single spiritual intelligence.</summary>
<keywords>Averroes, Aristotle, First Mover, celestial spheres, causality, divine perfection, cosmology, intelligence</keywords>

**FI.** My mind, weary of worldly business <note>original: "negotij mondani." This refers to the practical, everyday chores or social obligations Filone was attending to before Sofia stopped him.</note>, and forced into such base exercises, withdraws into itself for refuge.

**SO.** Why?

**FI.** Because he who knows the cause must know the effect. <note>Filone is using a classic principle of Aristotelian logic: if Sofia is the "cause" of his love, she should inherently understand the "effect" it has on his mind.</note>

**SO.** And how do you know that I know the cause of your meditations?

**FI.** I know that you know yourself more than anyone else.

**SO.** Even if I know myself—though not as perfectly as I would wish—I still do not know that I am the cause of your abstracted fantasies.

**FI.** It is the custom of you beautiful beloved ones, knowing the passion of your lovers, to pretend not to know it; but just as you are more beautiful and noble than the others, I would wish you to be more truthful as well; and since it is your nature to be without blemish, I wish that this common habit [of feigning ignorance] would not cause a defect in you.

**SO.** I see now, O Filone, that you find no other expedient to flee my accusations than by counter-accusing me: let us put aside whether I have notice of your passions or not; tell me clearly, what was making you so pensive just now?

**FI.** Since it pleases you that I express what you already know, I tell you that my mind, having withdrawn to contemplate (as is its habit) that beauty formed in you—which is imprinted in my mind as an image and is forever desired—has made me abandon my external senses.

**SO.** Ha, ha, you make me laugh: how can that which cannot enter through open eyes while standing present be imprinted in the mind with such efficacy? <note>Sofia is teasing him: she asks how his mind can "see" her internal image so intensely that it makes him blind to her actual physical person standing right in front of him.</note>

The third reason is because quality extends only to a limited space: but light extends through the diaphanous <note>original: "diafano"; refers to a transparent medium such as air or water.</note> without limit or measure. Fourth, because when the producer of a quality is removed, some impression of it always remains in the subject for some time—just as the heat of water remains after it is separated from the fire—but when the source of illumination is removed, nothing of the light remains in the diaphanous. Fifth, because a quality moves along with its subject, but light, as an illuminating force, does not move along with the movement of the air or water in which it resides. Sixth, many qualities of the same kind in a single object become confused and mixed, or they merge into one; however, many lights do not merge into one. You will see that if you walk toward two lamps, they produce two shadows, and if there are more, they produce more shadows. Furthermore, if three or more lamps are placed at a small opening from different directions, you will see that they project three distinct, opposite lights through that opening.

All these things show us that the light in the diaphanous, or in the illuminated body, is not a quality or a corporeal passion <term>passion: in classical philosophy, this refers to the state of being acted upon or undergoing a physical change from an external source.</term>; rather, it is a spiritual act activating the diaphanous through the representation of the source of illumination. It is separable by the removal of that source. Light assists the diaphanous in no different a way than the intellect, or the intellectual soul, assists the body; it has a connection with the body that is attendant or essential, but it cannot be mixed with it. Therefore, it is not changed by the changes of the body, nor is it corrupted by the body’s corruption. Thus, the true light is the intellectual light, which essentially illuminates both the corporeal and incorporeal worlds. In man, it gives light to the soul and to intellectual vision. ->### THIRD DIALOGUE ###<-

The Sun, among all corporeal things, is like the Divine Intellect among all spiritual things—its likeness and its true follower. Just as the light and vision of the human eye are dependent on and serve the intellectual light and its vision (with its many variations), so the light of the Sun depends on and serves the first and true light of the Divine Intellect. Just as supreme beauty consists in the Divine Intellect—in which the whole universe is most beautifully figured—so in the corporeal world, the Sun’s beauty is the supreme beauty, making the whole universe beautiful and bright.

*So.* The Sun is indeed a true image of the Divine Intellect, as is the eye of the human intellect, as you have said. Truly, the human intellect and the corporeal eye have a great similarity to the Divine Intellect and the Sun. For just as the Divine not only understands all the species <note>original: "specie"; in Renaissance philosophy, these are the "intelligible forms" or mental templates of all things.</note> of things within itself but also illuminates all other intellects with its bright and eternal ideas <note>original: "idee"; the archetypes in the mind of God.</note> (or species), so our intellect not only understands the species of all things but also illuminates all other cognitive faculties <note>original: "virtù conoscitive"; the various powers of the soul used for knowing, such as memory and imagination.</note> of man. This is so that even though their knowledge is particular and material, it may be directed by an intellect that is not brutish <note>original: "bestiale"; referring to the "sensitive soul" shared with animals, which lacks higher reason.</note> like that of other animals. Therefore, the eye and the Sun are not so similar, for the eye sees and does not illuminate, and the Sun illuminates and does not see.

And just as when the Moon is full and in opposition to the Sun, astrologers <note>In the Renaissance, the term "astrologer" (astrologhi) encompassed both astronomers and those who interpreted the stars' influence on human affairs</note> say it is then in a highly "inimical" <term>inimicabile: an astrological term for a "hostile" or discordant relationship between celestial bodies</term> aspect with the Sun; so too, when the soul takes all the light it has from the intellect into the lower part toward corporeality, it is in a hostile opposition to the intellect and distances itself from it entirely. 

The opposite occurs when the soul receives the light of the intellect in its upper, incorporeal part, facing that intellect; then it unites with it, just as the Moon does with the Sun during a conjunction <term>conjunction: "congiontione," the moment when the Moon is between the Earth and the Sun (the New Moon)</term>. It is certainly true that this divine union <note>original: "diuina copulatione"</note> causes it to abandon bodily things and the cares thereof; and thus the soul remains dark in the lower part facing us, like the Moon. And since contemplation and the union of the soul with the intellect have withdrawn it, bodily things are no longer appropriately provided for or managed by it. But so that the entire bodily part does not perish, the soul must by necessity depart from that union with the intellect, sharing its light with the lower part little by little, just as the Moon does after the conjunction. **SO.** And what is the meaning of there being two quarters?

The other is after the opposition <note>The Full Moon, symbolizing the soul's complete involvement in the material world</note>: and from this point, the upper part (which we cannot see) begins to overtake the lower part (which we do see) in light. And so it is in the soul when it moves from opposition back toward intellectual union: because once both parts are equal in light, the upper intellectual part begins to prevail, and reason defeats sensuality.

...tell me, what similarity does it have with the intellect? **FI.** In this way: the intellect is never deprived of, nor deficient in, its own intellectual light, as happens to the soul. This is because intellectual light belongs to the very essence of the intellect—without it, the intellect would have no being—whereas in the soul, this light is "participated" <term>participated: in Renaissance philosophy, this means the soul does not own the light inherently, but "takes part" in it by receiving it from a higher source</term> from that very intellect. That is to say, by coupling and uniting itself with the intellect, the soul receives all the intellectual light into its superior part, while its inferior, corporeal part remains in darkness. The body, no longer illuminated by the soul, loses its being, and the soul dissolves from it. **FI.** You have snatched the prey from your image, because it takes you away and forbids you entry; and in truth, you did not do it to benefit me, but rather out of fear. For if my life ended, your poison would end with it; and because you want my pain to be lasting, you do not want to allow the poison of your image to grant me death, for that pain is greater the longer it lasts.

**SO.** I do not know how to reconcile your words, O Filone: at one moment you make me divine and much desired by you; and at another you find me poisonous.

**FI.** Both are true, and both can coexist: for in you, the poisonous nature is caused by your divinity.

**SO.** How is it possible that evil comes from good?

**FI.** It can happen, but indirectly, because insatiable desire comes between them.

**SO.** In what way?

**FI.** Your beauty represents itself to me in a form more divine than human; but because it is always accompanied by a piercing and insatiable desire, it is converted within into a pernicious and very fierce poison. So it is that the more excessive your beauty is, the more it produces in me a more raging and poisonous desire. Your presence is a thriac to me only because it keeps me alive, but not to remove the poisonous nature and the pain; rather, it prolongs it and makes it more lasting. Because seeing you prevents my end—which would be the conclusion and rest for my burning desire—and...

<summary>Filone explains the paradox of his love: Sofia's divine beauty triggers an insatiable desire that acts as a poison, while her physical presence only serves to prolong his suffering by preventing the "mercy" of death.</summary>

# THIRD DIALOGUE

...that you understand me, but you would do me a pleasure if you would clarify them. **Phil.**
First, you ask whether love is generated—that is, proceeded from another—or if it is truly unbegotten, having never had any dependency on any predecessor. Second, you ask when it was born, assuming it is generated; whether its succession or dependency was from eternity or temporal; and if temporal, at what time it was born: whether perhaps it was born at the time of the creation of the world and the production of all things, or instead at some other time thereafter. The third thing you ask concerns the place in which it was born, and in which of the three worlds it had its origin: whether in the lower and terrestrial world, or in the celestial world, or perhaps in the spiritual world—that is, the angelic and divine. <note>Leone Ebreo utilizes the Neoplatonic concept of the "Three Worlds": the Sublunary (earthly), the Celestial (the stars and planets), and the Intellectual/Angelic (the realm of pure spirit).</note> Fourth, you ask who its parents were: that is, if it had only a father, or only a mother, or if it was born of both, and who they were; whether they were divine, human, or of another nature; and concerning them, what was its genealogy. And finally, fifth, you wish to know the end <note>The "end" here refers to the *causa finale* (final cause), a concept from Aristotelian physics meaning the purpose or goal for which a thing exists.</note> for which it was born into the world, and what necessity caused it to be born. For the final cause is that for which every produced thing was produced; and the end of the product is the first thing in the intention of the producer, even if it is the last in its execution. Are these, O Sofia, your five inquiries concerning the birth of love? **Soph.** These are they, certainly. I made the request, but you have expanded it in such a way that you give me great hope for the desired answer; for just as wounds that are well-opened and well-examined are better healed, so too are doubts more perfectly resolved when they are well-divided and taken apart. **SO. *On the other hand, I remember that you argued to me the other day—namely, that love is not always desire. For many times love is directed toward things that one already has and which exist, such as loving one’s father or children, the health one possesses, or the riches of those who own them; but desire is always for things that do not exist, or if they do exist, we do not have them. For that which is lacking is desired—to exist if it does not, and to be possessed if one does not have it. But the things or people we love are often present and we possess them, while we never love things that do not exist. Therefore, how can you say that all love is desire?***

**FI. *I also recall that we previously defined love differently than desire. For we said that desire is a voluntary effect <note>original: "effetto uolõtario." In this context, Philo refers to desire as a result or movement of the will.</note> of wanting to be or to have the thing esteemed as good which is lacking; and that love is a voluntary affection <term>affetto: an emotional state or "disposition" of the soul, distinct from a fleeting "effect"</term> to enjoy through union the thing esteemed as good, even if it is lacking. Nevertheless, we later declared that although desire is for something that is lacking, it nonetheless presupposes—just like love—some form of existence. Though a thing may be lacking in us, it exists in others, or in itself; if not in actuality <term>atto: the state of being fully realized or present</term>, then in potentiality <term>potentia: the capacity or power to exist or be acted upon</term>. And if it has no real existence, it has at least an imaginary and mental one. We have shown that love, despite sometimes being for a possessed thing, nonetheless always presupposes some lack of it, just as desire does. This is because the lover does not yet have perfect union with the beloved thing—hence they love and desire perfect union with it—or perhaps because, although they possess and enjoy <term>fruitione: the pleasure or "fruit" taken from possessing something good</term> it in the present, they lack the future enjoyment of it, and thus they desire it. So, in effect, if the matter is well considered...***

<summary>Sophia challenges Philo's definition of love as desire, arguing that we love things we already possess (like family or health), while Philo reconciles this by explaining that love always implies a desire for either a more perfect union or the continued possession of the object in the future.</summary>

->THIRD.<-

<meta>catchword: thing</meta>

*...desire and love are one and the same thing, despite the fact that in the common way of speaking <note>original: "uulgo," referring to the vernacular or common usage as opposed to philosophical precision.</note> each has some specific property, as you said; and therefore at the end of our previous discussion we defined love as being the desire for union with the beloved thing, and we declared how every desire is love, and every love is desire, and according to that I have currently defined love for you in general, which is the desire for something.*

So, the love of a thing possessed as well as that of a thing not possessed is one and the same as desire. But it is something other than delight, just as pain and sadness are different from hatred and abhorrence; for pain is from the possession of a present evil, while hatred is for not having it <note>Original: "per non hauerlo," implying the desire to avoid or be rid of the evil.</note>

Hope comes after love and desire, and it is directed toward a good thing that is in the future or currently separate from us. Fear is its contrary, directed toward a bad thing that is future or separate. When hope is joined with love or desire, the pursuit of the loved good thing follows; just as when fear is joined with hatred and abhorrence, the flight from the hated bad thing follows. The final result is joy and delight in a present and joined good thing, and its contrary is pain and sadness in a present and joined bad thing. This passion which is last in execution—namely, joy and delight in the good thing—is first in <term>intention: the mental goal or purpose that motivates an action before it begins</term>. For it is in order to achieve joy and delight that one loves, desires, hopes for, and pursues; and therefore, the soul finds its rest and peace in that joy. Since it is possessed in the present, it is loved and desired for the future. So, if one is philosophizing correctly, in whatever way you look at it, love and desire are essentially one and the same thing, even if in our manner of speaking one kind of love is more properly called "desire" and another more properly "love." And not only these two words, but others as well express this same reality; for in effect, what one loves, one sometimes feels affection for, esteems, chooses, <note>original: "s'affetta, si dilige, s'opta"</note> craves, and wills—and it is also thus desired. All these words and others like them, though each is applied more to one species of love than another, nevertheless in substance they all signify the same...

...the same thing: which is to desire the things that are lacking. For that which one possesses, in the moment it is possessed, is not sought after or loved <note>The author distinguishes between the act of wanting something new and the act of wanting to keep what you already have</note>; but it is always loved and desired to exist in the mind as a kind of good thing. Hence, the soul desires and loves that, if a thing does not exist, it should truly exist just as it does in the mind—that it should be in <term>act: the state of being fully realized or actually existing</term> as it is in <term>potentiality: the capacity to exist or become something</term>. In this way, perhaps, a father and son love each other: they desire to enjoy each other's presence in the future just as they do in the present. Likewise, the healthy man loves health and the rich man loves wealth; he does not only desire that they increase, but also that he may be able to enjoy them in the future as he does now. Therefore, love—just like desire—must be for things that are in some way lacking. This is why **Plato** defines love as the appetite for a good thing in order to possess it, and to possess it forever; for in that "forever" is included a continuous lack <note>original: "mancamento continuo"</note>. 

Although some continuous lack is joined with love, love nonetheless presupposes the "being" of the thing, because love is always for things that *are*. But desire is truly for things that are lacking, and many times for those things that do not yet exist. **FI.** In saying that love is for things that *are*, you speak the truth: because that which is not cannot be known, and that which cannot be known cannot be loved. But what you say—that desire is sometimes for things that do not exist, so that they may come to be—does not contain absolute truth. For that which in no way has being cannot be known, and that which cannot be known can even less be desired. Therefore...

**so.** Give me an example.

**Fi.** The name "knight" <note>original: "caualiere"</note> applies to anyone riding a four-legged beast, yet it is specifically reserved only for those who are skilled and expert in waging war on horseback. Likewise, the name "merchant" <note>original: "mercatante"</note> applies to anyone who buys anything at all, but they reserve it specifically for those whose own profession is the buying and selling of merchandise to make a profit. In this same way, "love" being a universal name for every desired thing, it is specifically applied to people or to significant things that have a more stable "being" within them. Of other things, one says they "desire" them and does not "love" them because their "being" is weaker; but in truth, all these things are loved.

**PHI.** Although in this specific love and desire it does not resemble it, it does indeed resemble it in this: that the father’s love consists largely in desiring for his son every good that he lacks. This presupposes a lack in the loved son, but not in the loving father. Likewise, the teacher desires virtue and wisdom <term>sapientia</term> <note>the Latin-derived term for wisdom, implying both intellectual knowledge and moral discernment</note> for the pupil, which are lacking in the pupil and not in the teacher; and one friend desires the happiness that the other friend lacks, wishing that he might have it and always enjoy it. It is quite true that these lovers, being mortal, gain a delightful joy <note>original: *allegrezza delettabile*</note> that they did not have before when their desire for the well-being of their loved ones is fulfilled. This does not happen in God, because no new joy, delight, or any other passion, or new change can come upon Him from...

<summary>Philo explains that God's love is like that of a father or teacher: it is a desire for the "good" of the beloved rather than a desire to fill a lack within Himself. Unlike human lovers, God's state of joy remains perfect and unchanged when this desire is fulfilled.</summary>

<header>THIRD.</header>

*...the new perfection of His beloved creatures: because He is free from every <term>passion</term> <note>In Renaissance philosophy, "passion" refers to being "acted upon" or affected by external things; God, being perfect, is considered "impassive."</note>, and is always immutable, and full of sweet delight, gentle joy, and eternal gladness. **SO.** *I like this discourse very much: but how will you reconcile me with Plato, who, being the authority that he is, denies that there is love in God?*

**PHI.** *Regarding that species of love which Plato discusses in his <term>Symposium</term> <note>original: *Convivio*; the dialogue where Plato explores the nature of Eros.</note>, which is only the kind of love shared among men, he speaks the truth when he says it cannot exist in God. However, regarding the <term>universal love</term> of which we speak, it would be false to deny its existence in God.*

**SO.** *Explain this difference to me.*

**PHI.** *Plato, in his Symposium, discusses only the kind of love that in humans is focused on the lover <note>original: *terminato nell'amante*; meaning the lover's own needs or benefits are the "end point" of the emotion.</note>, but not on the beloved. This is what is principally called "love," because that which is focused on the beloved is instead called <term>friendship and benevolence</term>. This first type he correctly defines as the "desire for beauty," and he says such love is not found in God; for whoever desires beauty does not possess it, nor is he beautiful. Since God is the <term>supreme beauty</term> <note>original: *sommo bello*</note>, He does not lack beauty, nor can He desire it; therefore He cannot possess love of that specific kind. But for us, who speak of love in its general sense, it is necessary to include both the love focused on the lover—which presupposes a <term>deficiency</term> <note>original: *mancamento*</note> in the lover—and the love focused on the beloved—which presupposes a deficiency in the beloved and not in the lover. For this reason, we have not defined love merely as the "desire for a beautiful thing" (as Plato did), but simply as desire...*

...[it is possible] that by a distorted intellect <note>original: *inferno d'ingegno*; likely a variant or typo for *infermo*, meaning a "sick" or "infirm" mind.</note> a thing may be considered bad, yet it does not cease to be truly and commonly good.

**SO.** And is it not the same with the beautiful?

**PHI.** Certainly not, because the beautiful is not one and the same to all men of sound judgment and virtue; for although the beautiful is considered good by everyone, to one virtuous man a thing is so beautiful that he is moved to love it, while to another virtuous man it is good, but not beautiful, nor is he moved to love it. And just as the good and the bad in the soul are like the sweet and the bitter to the sense of taste, so the beautiful and the non-beautiful in the soul are like the savory—that is, the delightful—and the unsavory to the taste. Furthermore, the ugly and the deformed are like the horrible and the abominable to the taste. 

Hence, just as one finds a thing that is sweet to all healthy people, but savory and delightful to one and not to another, so one finds a thing or person that is good in the eyes of every virtuous man, yet to another they are beautiful—so much so that their beauty incites him to love them—while to someone else, they are not. Therefore, you will see that <term>passionate love</term> <note>original: *amore passionabile*; a love driven by the passions or senses, which "stings" or causes suffering to the lover.</note>, which stings the lover, is always directed toward a beautiful thing. It is of this love alone that **Plato** speaks and defines as the **desire for the beautiful**—that is, the desire to unite with a beautiful person or a beautiful thing in order to possess it, such as a beautiful city, a beautiful garden, a beautiful horse, a fine falcon, a beautiful garment, or a beautiful jewel. 

These are things that one either desires to have, or, once they are had, one desires to continually enjoy them; and they always presuppose a lack, either in the present or in the future, within the person who loves. And of such love, Plato says that it does not exist in God—not that there is no love in God, but because such love cannot exist without <term>potentiality</term> <note>original: *potentia*; the philosophical concept of being "in potential," implying a lack of perfection or a state of becoming, which is incompatible with the nature of a perfect and fully realized God.</note>...

**PHI.** You are in error. **SO.** How will you deny to me that every beautiful thing is not also good? **PHI.** I do not deny it, but in common speech <note>original: "uolgarmente" refers to the common people or the vernacular understanding as opposed to philosophical precision.</note> it is usually denied. **SO.** In what way? **PHI.** They say that not every beautiful thing is good, because something that appears good is actually bad in effect; likewise, some things that appear ugly <note>The term "brutta" (ugly/foul) is the opposite of "bello" (beautiful) in this context.</note> are good. **SO.** That argument does not hold, for to whom a thing appears beautiful, it also appears good in that respect in which it is beautiful; and if it is good in effect, it is beautiful in effect; and that which appears ugly also appears bad in that respect in which it is ugly; and if it is good in effect, it is not ugly in effect. **PHI.** You refute them well, notwithstanding that, as I have told you, beauty has more of a place in appearance <note>term: <term>apparentia</term> (appearance) refers to how a thing is perceived by the senses.</note>, and goodness more in existence <note>term: <term>esistentia</term> (existence/essence) refers to the objective reality of a thing.</note>. It is indeed true that good and ugly cannot coexist in the same respect, but it is not true that everything that is not beautiful is ugly. **SO.** What is it then? **PHI.** It is neither beautiful nor ugly, as are many things among the number of good things. For you see well that among human persons, in whom beauty and goodness occur, some are found who are neither beautiful nor ugly; so much the more...

<summary>Philo and Sophia debate the relationship between beauty and goodness, concluding that while all beautiful things are good, not all good things (such as food or healthy air) are necessarily beautiful, as there exists a neutral state between beauty and ugliness.</summary>

Beauty is a grace that, by delighting the soul with the knowledge of it, moves the soul to love; and that good thing, or person, in whom such grace is found, is beautiful. But that good thing in which this grace is not found is neither beautiful nor ugly: it is not beautiful because it lacks grace; it is not ugly because it does not lack goodness. However, that which lacks both of these things—that is, grace and goodness—is not only not beautiful, but is evil and ugly. ### THIRD DIALOGUE ###

...or delight that the lover acquires through union with the beloved thing—whether it be in itself more worthy or less worthy—it makes him incline toward that beloved. But he does not thereby remain defective or of less dignity or perfection; rather, he gains more through the union and perfection of the beloved thing. Thus, not only is one who loves a person inclined toward them for the perfection or joy acquired in their union, but also one who loves not a person but some other thing inclines toward it to possess it, for the sake of what he gains in himself when he acquires it.

**SOPH.** I understand this, but what will you say when two have mutual love, and each is equally lover and beloved? You must admit that each of them is both inferior and superior to the other, which would be a contradiction.

**PHI.** It is not a contradiction; on the contrary, it is the truth. For each of them, insofar as they love, is inferior to the other, and insofar as they are loved, is superior to the other.

**SOPH.** Would each person then be superior to themselves?

**PHI.** This too is true: every lover is superior to themselves as the one beloved. And if perhaps one were to love oneself, their self-as-beloved would be superior to their self-as-lover. I have already told you, when we spoke of the commonality of love, that *Aristotle* (as *Averroes* <note>original: "Auerrois." Averroes was a 12th-century Islamic philosopher whose commentaries on Aristotle were foundational to Western thought.</note> sees it) maintains that God is the mover of the <term>first diurnal sphere</term> <note>The "Primum Mobile" or outermost sphere in the medieval cosmos, which rotates daily and moves all other spheres.</note>, which He moves for the love of something more excellent, just as each of the other <term>intellects</term> <note>In this cosmology, "intellects" are spiritual beings or angels that guide the movements of the celestial bodies.</note> moves the other spheres. And since nothing is more excellent than God—indeed, everything is inferior to Him—it must be said that God moves that highest sphere for the love of Himself. In God, it is more sublime to be loved by Himself than to love Himself, even though His <term>divine essence</term> <note>The fundamental nature of God.</note> consists of the purest unity, as you understood from me more extensively back then.

**SO.** And does this reasoning not seem sufficient to you, Philo?

**FI.** It does not seem right to me, nor did it even seem just to Socrates.

**SO.** Indeed? And why?

**FI.** Socrates, debating against the orator **Agathon** <note>Agathon was a tragic poet; his victory speech in the *Symposium* praised Love as the youngest and most beautiful of the gods.</note>, who still held love to be a great and most beautiful God, demonstrates that love is not a God, because he is not beautiful; for all gods are beautiful. And he demonstrates that he is not beautiful because love is the *desire for the beautiful*, and that which is desired is always lacking to the one who desires it, for one does not desire what one already possesses. Therefore, Socrates says that love is not a God, but is a **great demon** <note>original: "demone," referring to the Greek *daimon*. In this context, it refers to a mediatory spirit or "tutelary being" that exists between the mortal and divine realms.</note>, halfway between the superior gods and the inferior humans. And even if he is not beautiful like a God, he is not yet ugly like the inferior beings, but halfway between beauty and ugliness; for the desirer, even if he is not in **act** <term>act (atto): a state of completed reality or perfection; being "in act" means actually possessing a quality.</term> what he desires, he is still that thing in **potency** <term>potency (potentia): the capacity or potential to become or achieve a state that is not yet realized.</term>. And so, if love is the desire for the beautiful, it is beautiful in potency, and not in act, as the gods are.

**SO.** What do you wish to infer from this, Philo?

**FI.** I am showing you that divinity consists in the **beloved**, and not in the lover, because the beloved is beautiful in act like God, and the lover who desires him is beautiful only in potency. Through this desire, even if he makes himself divine, he is nevertheless not God like the beloved. And therefore, you will see that the beloved in the mind of the lover is honored, contemplated, and adored as his very God, and his beauty is reputed divine by the lover, so that no other can be equal to it. Does it not seem to you then, Sophia, that the beloved precedes the lover in excellence and as the cause of the lover's love, and is more worthy?

**SO.** Yes, certainly; but what will you say to the example of **Achilles** and **Alcestis**?

**FI.** **Alcestis**, who died for her beloved, was not honored as much as **Achilles**, who died for his lover; because the lover...

**SOPHIA.** I understand the reasons that moved Aristotle to make prime matter eternal, as well as the heavens themselves, the generation of things, circular motion, and time in a successive manner, one part following another. Does he perhaps have other reasons besides these to prove the eternity of the world?

**PHILO.** These I have told you are his natural reasons. The Peripatetics <note>Followers of Aristotle’s philosophy, named after the "peripatos" or covered walkways where they studied.</note> also offer two other theological reasons to prove that the world is eternal: one taken from the nature of the Maker, and the other from the purpose of His work.

**SOPHIA.** Make me understand this as well.

**PHILO.** They say that since the Maker, God, is eternal and immutable, the work—which is the world—must have been made from eternity <note>original: "ab eterno"</note> in one consistent way, because the thing made must correspond to the nature of the one who makes it. Furthermore, they argue that the purpose of the Creator in the creation of the world was nothing other than the desire to do good; why then should this "good" not have been performed always? For no impediment could ever intervene within the almighty God, who is supremely perfect.

**SOPHIA.** These reasons of the Peripatetics do not seem to be without force, especially the theological ones concerning the eternal nature of the divine Maker and the purpose of His voluntary production. What will the Platonists say—and all of us who believe the sacred Mosaic Law <note>A reference to the Torah or the Five Books of Moses, which begins with the creation of the world in Genesis.</note>—which places the creation of all things from nothing at the beginning of time?

**PHILO.** We others say many things in our defense: we agree that naturally, nothing can be made from nothing; however, miraculously, through divine omnipotence, we hold that things can indeed be made from nothing. This does not mean that "nothingness" is the material of things, in the way that wood is the material from which statues are made, but rather that God can make things anew, without the precedence of any matter whatsoever.

### THIRD BOOK

...you have: more besides. **Philo.** He <note>Referring to Plato.</note> judged that this formation of things—of the whole as well as of each individual part—was necessarily new [having a beginning in time], and not **from eternity** <note>original: "ab eterno"</note>. **Sophia.** Why? **Philo.** Because it is necessary for the formless to have existed before the formed. If you, Sophia, see a wooden statue, would you not judge that the wood was first found formless—lacking the shape of the statue—before it was shaped into it? **Sophia.** Yes, certainly. **Philo.** In the same way, **Chaos** <term>Chaos</term> <note>In this context, Chaos refers to "prime matter"—the raw, unstructured substance of the universe before God or a creator gave it order.</note> must be found formless before the world is formed. Thus, the formation of the world demonstrates its novelty and its being made anew; and the formlessness of that from which it was made demonstrates not novelty, but rather eternal antiquity. It follows then, and one must grant, that just as the formed world was made anew, so must we grant that the formless Chaos was never "new," but rather has had its being **from eternity**. You will then recognize the reason for that saying of the ancients: that **nothing makes nothing** <note>original: "niente fa niente." This is the famous philosophical principle *Ex nihilo nihil fit* (Nothing comes from nothing), which suggests that everything created must have a pre-existing material cause.</note>. For "making" implies a new formation, and form is relative to the formless from which it is made; for from no formlessness, no formed thing can be made. It is therefore necessary that, just as the formed world is made anew, the formless Chaos is produced **from eternity** by God. **Sophia.** Even if I grant you that Chaos has existed from eternity, I will not necessarily grant you that it is produced by God. **Philo.** You must grant it, because Chaos is formless and imperfect, and one must assign it a productive cause that is the most universal Form and Perfection—just as Chaos is the most universal formlessness and imperfection. That cause is God. **Sophia.** How? Does God have form? Then He would be formed and made anew, which is absurd. **Philo.** God is not formed, nor does He have form,

<summary>Philo explains that for the world to be "formed," there must have been an eternal, formless material (Chaos) already in existence, as nothing can be created from nothing. He argues that this eternal Chaos is an imperfect product of God, whom he defines as the ultimate, universal Form and Perfection.</summary>

Hence it is necessary that either both be from eternity—that is, form and matter, and the whole world (as Aristotle says)—or else both and all are created anew, as **the faithful** <note>The "faithful" refers to those following religious traditions (Christian, Jewish, or Islamic) who believe God created both matter and the universe out of nothing at a specific point in time.</note> hold. And thus in one way or the other, matter is first in natural origin, but not in temporal anticipation, as Plato suggests.

**Philo.** That matter holds a natural priority to form, as the subject is to the thing of which it is the subject, this is manifest: but beyond this, one must grant that matter is also first in time—before every time and formation—which Aristotle himself shows; because matter must first in time be in **potentiality** <term>potentiality</term> <note>original: "potentia." ### ->THIRD DIALOGUE<-

is nothing other (as **Aristotle** says) than totally removing the nature of matter and of potentiality <term>potentiality</term> <note>The capacity of matter to take on different forms.</note>.

**SO.** How then does **Aristotle** posit that the formed world is eternal?

**FI.** Because he does not place **prime matter** <term>prime matter</term> <note>The most basic, formless substance that underlies all physical reality.</note> as common to the entire world, but only in the lower world of **generation and corruption** <note>The sublunary world (Earth), where things are born and die.</note>. In this lower world, he posits that prime matter is eternal, and that no single form is co-eternal with it; rather, each form is new within it through generation, and another is reborn through corruption. He posits an eternal succession of many and diverse forms, with eternal generation and corruption; yet each individual thing is newly generated and corruptible.

**SO.** In the heavens then, where there is no generation, **Aristotle** will not place matter?

**FI.** In no way does he want the heavens and the stars to have substantial matter; for if they had it, they would be subject to generation and corruption, like the lower bodies. Instead, they are simply an eternal body, which is matter for movement, but not for generation.

**SO.** And why does **Plato** not posit that eternal matter is eternally formed, and by a succession of forms?

**FI.** To **Plato** it seems impossible that a formed body is not made of formless matter; hence the heaven, the Sun, and the stars—which are beautifully formed—he affirms to be made of formless matter, just like all the lower bodies.

**SO.** And is the matter of the celestial bodies perhaps the same as that of the lower ones, or another kind?

**FI.** It cannot be other than prime matter, which is in every way formless, for there is no reason why it should be multiplied or diversified from another; it must be one and the same in all things composed of matter. And it seems right to him that the whole world, just as it has a common father who is **God**, should also have a mother common to all

### THIRD BOOK ###

...you indissoluble, because my strengths are greater than your fragility. <note>original: "te indissolubili, perche maggiore sono mie forze che uostra fragilità." This is a paraphrase of the Demiurge's speech in Plato’s Timaeus, where God promises to hold the universe together despite its natural tendency to decay.</note> But I believe that with these words **Plato** does not mean that the heavens are eternally indissoluble; rather, he intends to show the reason why they are not continuously being born and decaying—remaining short-lived like the lower bodies—despite being all made of one same matter, which is the cause of both novelty and dissolution. He says that although by their material nature they ought to be perishable, nonetheless, because of their greater **formal beauty** <term>formal beauty</term> <note>In Platonic philosophy, "form" is the divine blueprint or essence that gives matter its identity; "formal beauty" suggests the heavens reflect the divine mind more perfectly than Earth does.</note> which is shared greatly by God, they are extremely long-lasting.

**SO.** Therefore the heavens are destined to dissolve, according to **Plato**.

**FI.** They are.

**SO.** And can you tell me when he believes this will happen?

**FI.** When they finish their natural lifespan, which has been limited for them—just as it is for each of the lower bodies—though theirs is much more durable.

**SO.** Is there anyone who has assigned them a specific limit of time?

**FI.** Indeed, the theologians more ancient than **Plato**, whose disciple he was, say that the lower world decays and renews itself every **seven thousand years**. <note>This refers to the "Cosmic Week" theory, common in ancient Near Eastern and Jewish thought, where the world exists for six thousand years of activity and one thousand years of rest or "Sabbath."</note>

**SO.** And how long does it remain in this state of decay?

**FI.** Of the seven thousand years, they say that for six thousand years the **Chaos** of the lower bodies is always germinating; and once these have finished, gathering everything back into itself, it rests in the seven-thousandth year. In that interval, it becomes pregnant with a new germination for another six thousand years.

**SO.** And how many of these seven thousand years have we already passed?

**FI.** We are, according to the **Hebrew truth** <note>original: "uerità Hebraica." This refers to the tradition of calculating time from the biblical creation of the world (Anno Mundi).</note>, at five thousand two hundred and sixty-two years from the beginning of creation. When the six thousand years are finished, the lower world will decay.

**SO.** And what will cause it to decay?

**FI.** The corruption will be caused by the predominance of one of the **four elements**, most especially fire, or perhaps water. <note>Referring to the ancient belief that the world would end in either a Great Conflagration (fire) or a Great Flood (water) when the balance of nature shifted.</note>

The text says: "in the year of the Jubilee each shall return to his origin and root" <note>original: "nell'anno del Iubileo ciascuno tornarà alla sua origine, e radice"; a paraphrase of Leviticus 25:13.</note>. Liberty would be proclaimed in the land, so that in that year, past things were extinguished, and a new world began for fifty years, like the past one. They say this Jubilee signifies the fiftieth thousandth year, in which the whole world is renewed—the celestial as well as the lower. I could tell you many other things about this, but this should suffice to give you some notice of the position of these theologians, and the reason for their audacity in the limitation of the times and the life of the world.

**SO.** How can they draw Moses to their opinion, who clearly says that "in the beginning God created the heaven and the earth," which seems to place the creation of Chaos together with all the rest?

**PH.** We read the text differently. This word, "in the beginning," in Hebrew <note>The Hebrew word is *Bereshit*.</note> can mean "before." You would say, then: "before God created and separated the heaven and the earth from Chaos"—that is, the terrestrial and celestial world—the earth (that is, Chaos) was empty and void. ...were to become another, and thus always in continuous succession all made by an eternal hand, it is more reasonable than the opinion which posits that this order had a beginning, and that before it there was nothing. For the former posits an eternal successive order in the generation of the world, and concedes that **nothing is made from nothing** <note>original: "di nulla non si fa cosa alcuna"; this refers to the classical philosophical principle *ex nihilo nihil fit*, which argues that matter cannot be created out of absolute nothingness.</note>, while this other opinion does not imply this. Thus, against that [Platonic] opinion, the strongest arguments of its opponents have no place—such as the argument that nothing comes from nothing, or that **first matter** <term>first matter</term> <note>The most basic, formless substance that exists before it is shaped into specific things like earth, water, or air.</note> cannot be newly made or generated. **Plato** himself concedes and presupposes these propositions, as well as those two theological arguments regarding the divine work: that it must be eternal, just as He is the **Artificer** <term>Artificer</term> <note>Italian: *opifice*. A term for God as the supreme craftsman or "Demiurge" who shapes the universe.</note>. And thus, the end [or result] of His work, which is good, must be eternal; both of these propositions Plato concedes insofar as they pertain to the divine agent.

But he says that God grants His eternity to that which is capable of enjoying it, such as the **Intellect**, in which are the **Ideas**, and **first matter**, which is **Chaos**. For the one is **pure act** and form, and the other is **pure potential** <note>In Aristotelian philosophy, "pure act" is perfect realization (God/Intellect), while "pure potential" is the capacity to become anything (Matter/Chaos) but having no shape of its own.</note> and matter that is entirely formless; the one is the universal father of all things, and the other the common mother to all. These alone have been able to participate in divine eternity, having been produced by Him from eternity. But their children—who, through these two parents, are made and formed by God, such as the entire universe and every one of its parts—are not capable of eternity. For everything made is "formed," which is to say, composed of the matter of **Chaos** and the form of the intellectual **Idea**; and it is necessary that they have a temporal beginning and end, as I told you above. Thus, the work and the end in the divine production...

V 4

...answer the second question, regarding when love was born and what was the first love.

**Philo:** The first love is that of the first lover for the first beloved. But since neither of these was ever born—rather, both are eternal—one must also say that their love, which is the first love, was never born. Instead, it is eternal just as they are, produced from eternity by them both.

**Sophia:** Tell me who the first beloved and the first lover are; by knowing them, I will know what the first love is.

**Philo:** The first lover is God, knowing and willing; the first beloved is God himself, the supremely beautiful.

**Sophia:** Then the first love is God’s love for himself.

**Philo:** Yes, certainly.

**Sophia:** Many absurd and contradictory things would follow from this. First, the **simplest divine essence** <term>divine essence</term> <note>The fundamental nature of God. In medieval and Renaissance philosophy, God was considered "simple," meaning His nature is a perfect whole without separate parts or divisions.</note> would be divided into a part that is loved but does not love, and a part that loves but is not loved. Second, God as lover would be inferior to himself as beloved; for, as you have shown me, every lover, insofar as he is a lover, is inferior to his beloved. This is because if love is a **desire for union** (as you have said), God, in loving, would desire to unite with himself. Since he is always one with himself, this would suggest that God lacked himself. Such a love would presuppose a deficiency, and many other similar inconsistencies would follow. I will not dwell on them, for they will be obvious to you and to anyone who has understood the conditions you have placed on love.

**Philo:** It is not permitted, O Sophia, to speak of the intrinsic love of God as lover and beloved with the same tongue and the same lips with which we are accustomed to speak of worldly loves. In Him, being beloved and being lover creates no diversity <note>original: "diversità," here meaning division or a lack of unity</note> at all; rather, this intrinsic relationship creates the...

...its most perfect and simple unity: because His **essence** <term>essence</term> <note>The fundamental nature of a thing; what it is in itself.</note> would not be of the highest life if there did not reverberate within itself—from the beauty or **wisdom** <term>wisdom</term> <note>original: "sapientia"</note> that is beloved—the wise lover, and from both of them, the most excellent love. This makes the receiver faithful, even if it cannot grasp the entire nature of the thing received. Likewise, it is enough for our intellectual mirror to receive and form an image of the immense divine essence, according to its capacity...

This unity, in its highest simplicity, contains the nature of the beloved, the lover, and the love without any multiplication or division—just as the light of the Sun contains all the essences of particular lights and colors within a single and eminent clarity. [unifying], because since love is the cause of the birth of the world, the proper and immediate cause must be present when the effect is, and the effect when the cause is. **SO.** In what way is love the cause of the birth of the world? **FI.** The world, like every other thing made and generated, is born from two parents—a father and a mother—from whom it could not be generated except through the love of one for the other, which unites them in the generative act. **SO.** Who are these two parents, or progenitors? **FI.** The first parents are God, as I have already told you, and they are the Supreme Beauty, or the Supreme Good (as Plato calls it), who is the true Father, the first beloved; and the lover is one with the divinity, or Wisdom—or let us say a division <note>original: "divisione". Here, Philo likely refers to the first distinction or emanation within the Divine unity.</note>—which, knowing its own division, loves and produces intrinsic love; and the first Mother with the Father is one and the same within that divinity. Thus, as the divinity loved its own beauty, it desired to produce a child in its own likeness; this desire was the first extrinsic love—that is, the love of God toward the world produced—which, when it was born, caused the first production of the world’s first parents and of the world itself. **SO.** Whom do you call the other parents of the world? **FI.** The two first ones generated by God in the creation of the world: that is, the First Intellect <term>First Intellect</term> <note>In Neoplatonic thought, the first emanation from God, containing the archetypes of all things.</note>, in which all the Ideas <term>Ideas</term> <note>The eternal, perfect forms or patterns of which all earthly things are mere shadows.</note> of the supreme craftsman shine, who is the forming Father and generator of the world; and the shadowy Chaos <term>Chaos</term> <note>The primordial, unformed matter that receives the "forms" or "Ideas" to become the physical world.</note> of the shadows of all the Ideas, which contains all their essences, which is the Mother of the world. Through these two, as the first parental instruments, God—acting as a desiring love—created, formed, and painted the entire world in the likeness of divine beauty and wisdom, or rather, the divine essence.

And so the plants, which are the least perfect of living things, lacking beauty greatly, do not desire it because they do not know it, except for that small amount that belongs to their natural perfection. love for the good, which they <note>Referring to the "inferior things" mentioned on the previous page.</note> lack compared to that which man possesses; this is because their knowledge of that missing beauty is meager, and extends only to their sensory comforts. And for this reason, **Pythagoras** <note>Pythagoras is traditionally credited with coining the term "philosopher" (lover of wisdom) to distinguish humans from the gods, who are truly wise.</note> called wise men "philosophers"—that is, lovers or desirers of wisdom—because he who possesses more wisdom is better able to recognize what he still lacks of its perfection, and thus desires it all the more. Since **wisdom** is much broader and deeper than the human intellect, one who swims further into its divine sea better understands its vastness and depth; thus, he desires even more to reach its perfect limits, so far as is possible for him. Its water is like salt water: the more one drinks of it, the more it creates thirst. For the delights of wisdom are not satiating like all other delights; rather, they become more desirable and insatiable with every passing hour. 

Therefore, **Solomon** <note>Leone Ebreo is referencing Proverbs 5:19. **FI.** Do not be deceived by the literal property of the word "infinite," which signifies an undetermined and imperfect quantity, from which divine beauty is very remote. We cannot speak of God and of incorporeal things except with words that are somewhat corporeal; for our very language and speech is, in itself, corporeal. Even to say "perfect" is an inadequate word for the divinity, because it literally means "entirely made" <note>original: "interamente fatto"; the Italian *perfetto* comes from the Latin *perfectus*, meaning "thoroughly made." Filone argues that since God was never "made," the word is technically a misfit.</note>, and in the divinity there is no "making" at all. 

However, we use the word "perfect" to mean that which is free of every defect and which contains every perfection. And we use the word "infinite" to mean that the perfection, wisdom, and beauty of God the Creator is disproportionate and incomparable to every other created perfection. For He who created everything from nothing must exceed His creatures in perfection—creatures who, by themselves, are nothing—just as much as the Supreme Being exceeds pure nothingness. This is an incommensurable excess, without any proportion or comparison; this we call infinite, although in...

**Vocabulary:**
*   **Divine beauty**: the absolute, spiritual beauty of God.
*   **Infinite**: here used to mean "beyond comparison" rather than "unending size."
*   **Perfect**: used here to mean "lacking nothing" rather than "completed."
*   **Incorporeal**: spiritual; lacking a physical body.
*   **Creator God**: the source of all existence.
*   **Perfection**: the state of having all possible excellence.

Explain to me these two kinds of lack—that is, the privative and the productive of love—and the difference between the one and the other. **FILONE** <gloss>Fi.</gloss> The lack of every perfection can occur in only two ways. Either there is still a potential for that perfection—which is properly called "deficiency"—or else both the actualization and the potential are missing together; and they call this **priva-**

<summary>Filone distinguishes between two types of "lack": a privative lack, which is a true defect, and an incitative lack, which drives desire and is actually a sign of perfection in the angelic world.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the philosophical dialogue between Filone and Sofia regarding the nature of beauty and desire. Filone is explaining the distinction between two types of "lack" (privation): one that retains the potential to be filled, and one that is absolute. This distinction is crucial to his argument that the "angelic world" possesses a higher form of desire for God's beauty because it has a greater awareness of what it lacks.</meta>

### T H E O R Y.
<meta>catchword: lower</meta>

...absolute [privation]. **SOFIA** <gloss>So.</gloss> Give me an example of both. **FILONE** <gloss>Fi.</gloss> In artificial things, you will see a piece of raw wood which lacks the form and beauty of a statue of Apollo; nonetheless, it is in **potentiality** <term>potentia: the inherent capacity of a thing to become something else or to acquire a new quality</term> toward it. However, a portion of water, just as it is deprived in **act** <term>atto: the state of being fully realized or actually existing in a specific form</term> of the form of a statue, so too is it deprived in potentiality: for a statue cannot be made of water as it can of wood. That first failing, which is not stripped of potentiality, is called a "lack"; this other, which lacks the potentiality along with the act, is called **absolute privation** <note>original: "assoluta priuatione." In Aristotelian philosophy, this is a total absence of a quality in a subject that has no natural capacity to possess it.</note>. 

And in natural things, the **prime matter** <term>materia prima: the most fundamental, formless reality that underlies all physical things</term> that is currently in the form of fire or water, even if it lacks the form and essence of air in act, nevertheless does not lack it in potentiality; for air can be made from fire, and likewise from water. Nonetheless, [this matter] lacks the form of the stars, the Sun, the Moon, or the celestial world, not only in act but also in potentiality, because prime matter possesses neither the potentiality nor the **passibility** <note>The capacity to be acted upon or changed by an external force.</note> to become the heavens or a star. 

This same difference exists in the lack of beauty when comparing the angelic world to the corruptible one. In the angels, their failing is a failing in act only, but they do not lack in knowledge and inclination—which is like the potentiality found in prime matter. And just as in prime matter the lack of the act gives it an inclination and desire for every form for which it has potentiality, so too the angelic cognition and inclination toward the supreme beauty—which they lack—gives them the most intense love and most ardent desire. This failing is not absolute privation, because whoever knows and desires what they lack is not entirely deprived of it: for knowledge is a potential existence of that which is lacking, and so too are love and desire. But in the **lower** <note>The text cuts off here at the catchword "riore," referring to the "mondo inferiore" or lower/physical world.</note> world...

<summary>Filone explains the difference between a "lack" that retains potential (like wood becoming a statue) and "absolute privation" (like water's inability to be a statue). He argues that angels have a "lack" of supreme beauty that is filled with potentiality and knowledge, which drives their intense love and desire.</summary>
