### D I A L O G U E

...lower [world] where there is no such knowledge and desire for this highest beauty; along with the **act** <term>atto: the state of being fully realized or actually existing</term>, the **potentiality** <term>potentia: the inherent capacity to acquire a quality</term> for this is also missing. Such a deficiency is **absolute privation** <note>original: "priuatione assoluta." A total absence in something that isn't even capable of receiving the quality.</note> and a true defect. It is not, however, a "cognitive" deficiency—one that incites and produces love—for that kind of lack is a perfection in created things. Indeed, in the most excellent things, this [cognitive] deficiency is found to be greater, more aware, and more inciting of love than it is in the corruptible world, while the "privative" deficiency is lesser. In the corruptible world, the opposite is true: the inciting deficiency is lesser, and the privative deficiency is greater; thus, it is less perfect and more defective.

**SOFIA** <gloss>SO.</gloss> I see well the difference between the deficiency of beauty that is cognitive and productive of love—which is found more in the intellectual world—and that of the privative sort, stripped of knowledge and love, which is found more in the corruptible world. I recognize that one implies perfection and the other defect. But three things remain doubtful to me:

First, that the deficiency of the lower world cannot be called absolutely privative, because even in that world, the highest beauty is known and is desired by men, who are a part of it.

Second, that this cognitive and desiring deficiency of the highest beauty does not seem able to coexist with being "in potentiality" for the thing that is lacking "in act," as you have said; for potentiality can be reduced to act, and yet no finite beauty can ever possess infinite beauty—which is what you say it knows and desires.

The third, which seems strange to me, is that **God** in any created thing would put knowledge and desire for something they lack and which is impossible for them to acquire, as would be the case with what you say regarding the **angelic world**. Resolve these doubts for me, O Filone, so that [my mind] might better be

...will quiet your mind on this matter of where love was born.

**FILONE** <gloss>Fi.</gloss> I expected such doubts from you, and they are quite appropriate; for through their solution, you will more fully understand that love was born in the angelic world, as I have told you. 

Regarding your first point, I tell you that in this corruptible world <note>the physical world characterized by change, decay, and death</note> there is no clear knowledge of the supreme divine beauty. This is because such beauty cannot be perceived except by an **intellect in act** <term>intelletto in atto: an intellect that is actively engaged in thought and fully realized, as opposed to one that merely has the potential to think</term> that is separated from matter. Such an intellect acts as a mirror capable of receiving the transfiguration of divine beauty. 

This kind of intellect is not found in the lower world. The mixed elements, inanimate objects, plants, and animals all lack intellect entirely; and man, who does possess it, has it only as a **potential intellect** <term>intelletto potentiale: the human capacity for reason that must be developed through experience and study</term>. This human intellect understands the essences of things by drawing them from the senses. The highest level to which it can rise—even when nourished by true wisdom—is to arrive at a knowledge of incorporeal essences by means of bodily ones. 

For instance, through the movement of the heavens, we come to know their **movers** <note>In Renaissance cosmology, it was believed that celestial spheres were moved by spiritual beings or "intelligences."</note>, which are both physical and intellectual powers; and through this sequence, we come to a knowledge of the **First Cause** <note>The ultimate source of all existence, usually identified as God.</note> as the first of all movers. But this is like seeing the bright body of the Sun reflected in water or through some other transparent medium; our weak sight cannot look directly at the Sun itself. 

In this same way, our human intellect sees incorporeal things through bodily ones. Although it knows that the First Cause is immense and infinite, it knows this only through its effect, which is the physical universe; through the work, it knows the Master. It does not know Him directly through Himself by seeing His own mind and art, as the angelic world does. Because those beings are intellects separated from matter, they are capable of seeing—or rather, having impressed upon them directly and immediately—the clear divine beauty.

### T H I R D.

*...in life, no one other than Moses has achieved it.*

**SO.** I have sufficiently understood the solution to the first doubt; I would like you to resolve the second for me: how can it be that an angel has the **potential** <term>potential: the capacity to become or achieve something that is not yet fully realized</term> for a desire-led knowledge of infinite beauty, which is impossible for it to ever acquire in **act**? <term>act: the full realization or completion of a capacity; "in act" means actually possessing the thing sought</term>

**FI.** It is impossible for the finite to become infinite, just as it is impossible for the creature to be made the creator. Regarding such an acquisition, one does not find a potential in the souls of the blessed <note>referring to those who have achieved eternal life in the presence of the Divine</note> to become infinite themselves; rather, they have the potential to couple and unite themselves with the infinite beauty of God, even though they remain finite. Their knowledge of His immense beauty serves this purpose, and their love and inclination direct them toward it.

**SO.** How can the infinite be known by the finite? And how can infinite beauty be imprinted upon a finite mind?

**FI.** This is not strange, because the thing known exists and is imprinted in the knower according to the mode and nature of the knower, not according to the nature of the thing known. Look how the entire hemisphere <note>the visible half of the celestial sphere or the sky</note> is seen by the eye and is imprinted within the tiny pupil—not according to its celestial size and nature, but according to what the size and power of the pupil is capable of. Likewise, infinite beauty is imprinted in the finite angelic or blessed mind, not according to the mode of its own infinity, but according to the finite capacity of the mind that knows it. Thus the eye of the Eagle <note>a traditional symbol for the highest intellectual or spiritual vision, as the eagle was believed to be the only creature able to look directly at the sun</note> sees the bright, great Sun directly and is transfigured by it—not as the Sun is in itself, but as the eye of the Eagle is capable of receiving it. There is another kind of knowledge of the immense divine beauty that is equal to the beauty itself: that is the knowledge which the highest God has of His own highest beauty. It is as if the Sun, with all its visible brilliance, were to see itself.

# THEORIZIO.
**Y 4**

Therefore, although they [the angels] are incorporeal and do not possess physical motion, they possess intellectual motion toward their first cause and final end, through successive contemplation and union <note>original: "copulatione." In this context, it refers to the spiritual and intellectual joining of the mind with God.</note>. This succession is what the philosophers call the **angelic aevum**, <term>aevum: a philosophical concept of time that exists between human time (linear and changing) and divine eternity (perfectly still). It is the "time" of eternal beings like angels who do not age but can have a sequence of thoughts.</term> which is the middle ground between the time of the corporeal world and divine eternity. Within such succession, there can exist intellectual potential, love, and desire, as well as a successive and unitive adherence (as I have already told you). 

Even if I were to grant you that they are always at a single degree of union, there would still be no lack of love and desire for the continuation of that union for eternity. As I have told you, good things already possessed are loved by desiring to enjoy them forever with perpetual delight; thus, angelic love is always directed toward divine beauty, both intensively and extensively. 

**SO.** I am satisfied regarding the second doubt, and somewhat regarding the third. 

**FI.** Based on what was said in the solution to the second doubt, the solution to the third is manifest. I grant you that God and Nature do not place within any creature a complete love or desire—or even an inclination or inherence—except toward achieving what is a possible thing, and never toward the purely and manifestly impossible. 

Therefore, you will see that a man does not desire to walk with his feet into heaven, or to fly with wings, or to be a star, or to hold a star in his hand, nor other similar things. Even though these things are worthy, and the man lacks them, and their worthiness is well known, they are nevertheless not desired because their impossibility is manifest. Where the hope of achieving a thing is missing, desire is also missing; for it is the hope of acquiring a delightful thing—when it is known and found to be lacking—that incites love and the desire to acquire it. # DIALOGUE

...where hope is sluggish, love is never intense, nor is desire ardent; and when hope is absent because the acquisition is impossible, the love and the desire of the knower are also absent. But the love and the angelic desire to enjoy the immense divine beauty is not for a thing impossible or desperate for them, because (as I have told you) they can, and do hope to, attain and enjoy it as their own happiness. Toward that beauty they always direct and turn themselves, as their own end, notwithstanding that it is infinite and the angels are finite.

**SO.** I have well understood the solution to the third doubt, and I see that you add a fourth condition to love: that besides the requirement that it be for something beautiful, and known by the lover, and that it in some way is lacking or could be lacking to them, it must also (according to you) be possible to attain it, and there must be hope of acquiring it. This seems reasonable; but we find experience to the contrary, and we see that men naturally desire never to die—a thing which is impossible, manifest, and without hope.

**FI.** Those who desire it do not entirely believe that it is impossible. They have heard from the sacred histories <note>original: "historie legali." This refers to the Holy Scriptures or the "Books of the Law" (the Torah/Pentateuch and related biblical accounts).</note> that Enoch, Elijah, and also Saint John the Evangelist are immortal in body and soul. Although they see that this was achieved by a miracle, everyone thinks that God could perform a similar miracle for them. And so, with this possibility joined to some remote hope, it incites a sluggish desire—especially because death is horrible, and one's own corruption <note>The breakdown and decay of the physical body.</note> is odious to anyone who wishes to exist. Furthermore, the desire is not to acquire a new thing, but rather not to lose the life that one already finds within themselves; which, being possessed in the present, makes it an easy thing to deceive... <meta>catchword: ...one's self (from "ingannare")</meta>

<meta>This page continues the dialogue where Philo (Filone) is responding to Sophia’s observation that humans naturally desire physical immortality, which seems impossible. Philo is explaining that while physical immortality is impossible, the desire itself points to a deeper truth about the soul.</meta>

### BOOK THREE

...leads man to desire that he not be lost, even if it is naturally impossible. This desire is so sluggish that it can be for an impossible and imaginary thing, because it is of such great importance to the one who desires it. And I will also tell you that the foundation of this desire is not vain in itself, even if it is somewhat deceptive. For man's desire to be immortal is truly possible, because the essence of man (as <note>original: "Platon"</note> Plato rightly holds) is nothing other than his <term>intellective soul</term> <note>In Renaissance philosophy, this refers to the highest part of the human soul—the rational and spiritual faculty that is capable of understanding universal truths and connecting with the divine.</note>. Through virtue, wisdom, knowledge, and divine love, this soul becomes glorious and immortal.

Those who are in torment I do not call entirely immortal, because that pain is the deprivation of the <term>divine vision</term> <note>Also known as the Beatific Vision; the direct experience of God's presence which serves as the ultimate goal of human existence.</note>, which for the soul can be considered a form of mortality, even if it is not entirely annihilated. Men are deceived into thinking that their physical being is their true essence, and so they believe that the natural desire for immortality applies to the physical body. In truth, this immortality belongs only to spiritual things, as I have told you. 

From this, O Sophia, you will understand the certainty of the human intellective soul: if man were not truly immortal according to the intellective soul—which is the true man—all men would not desire immortality as they do. Other animals, just as they are entirely mortal, do not think about, do not know, do not desire, and do not hope for immortality. Perhaps they do not even know what mortality is, even though they flee from harm and pain. Since the knowledge of opposites is one and the same <note>Philo refers to the philosophical principle that the mind understands a concept (like life) through its opposite (like death).</note>, the man who knows death also knows and seeks his immortality—that is, the immortality of his soul. And he would not do this if it were not possible to achieve it in the way I have described.

-># THEORIZING<-

[Plato] places its principle among the lower gods, that is, the demons: whose beauty is in **potentiality** <note>In Aristotelian philosophy, "potentiality" is the capacity to become something, whereas "actuality" is the state of being fully realized.</note> compared to the angelic beauty, which is in **actuality**. Just as Plato posits the **Ideas** as the principles for actual perfections, sciences, and human wisdom in actuality, so too for the potentialities, virtues, and passions of the soul, he posits the lower elements of the gods as principles. Since love is (as I have told you) the primary passion of the soul, he posits a great and primary **demon** <note>original: "demone". Following the Platonic tradition, a "daimon" is a spirit acting as a bridge between the divine and the mortal, not a malevolent entity.</note> as its principle. 

But the love we are speaking of is not a bodily passion in the angels, but an **intellectual inherence** <note>A profound spiritual attachment or bond.</note> in supreme beauty. Therefore, this love exceeds both demons and men together; it is the principle of love in the created world. Plato does not deny this, because he himself places love in the supreme God, shared with the other gods, just as the demon's love is shared with humans. But because it is so much higher than the latter, he does not speak of them both as one common thing, as we have done here.

SO. I am now satisfied regarding this last doubt. I would only like to know from you, in this part, how the love that was born in the angelic world proceeds from there and is shared with the entire created universe; and whether all angels participate in the love of divine beauty immediately, or if they do so through one another, each through the one superior to him.

**FI.** You judge well; and in effect, he wants us to sense that he contradicts himself so that we might seek out the intended cause.

**SO.** What does he wish to signify?

**FI.** Ordinary commentaries struggle literally to reconcile this text by saying that first he spoke of the creation of both in summary, and afterward he describes the manner at length—how the woman was made from the side of the man. *sin, he was divided into two halves, as you have understood.*

**SOPHIA:** I am pleased to see that Plato has drunk from the waters of the sacred spring <note>original: "sacro fonte"; a metaphor suggesting Plato was influenced by the Hebrew Bible</note>; but where does this difference come from, that he makes the division <note>original: "incisione"</note> of man happen because of a preceding sin, contrary to the sacred history <note>the Book of Genesis</note>, which places the division as a help for man, and the sin following after?

**PHILO:** The difference is not as great as it seems, if you consider well that Plato, in this matter, wishes to be an interpreter of the sacred history rather than a contradictor of it.

**SOPHIA:** In what way?

**PHILO:** In effect, it is sin that divides man and causes division within him, just as righteous uprightness makes him one and preserves his union. And yet we can also say with truth that man's being divided makes him sin: because as long as he is united, he has no inclination to sin, nor to depart from his union. Thus, because sin and the division of man are almost the same thing—or rather, they are inseparable and interchangeable—one can say that sin comes from division, as the Holy Scripture says, or that division comes from sin, as Plato says.

**SOPHIA:** I would like you to explain the reason for this agreement <note>original: "conformità"</note> more clearly, and how the Hebrew history is understood first, and then the Platonic fable.

**PHILO:** First, man being created as a male joined with a female, as I have told you, has no way to sin; for the serpent could not deceive the woman while she was joined with the man, as he did once she was separated from him. Once the division was made, it immediately presents the deception of the serpent, and the sin of ***Adam*** and ***Eve***, and their punishment.

So, according to the manner of the Hebrew history, it was necessary for the division to precede the sin. But the Platonic fable, although it is derived from the Hebrew, is both one with it and yet of a different fashion; for it places the sin within the joined man for wanting to fight against the gods; whence, as punishment for his arrogance, he was cut and divided in two, male and female. It presents the arrangement of the genitals as a remedy for their perishing, as you have heard. And if you knew, O Sophia, the allegorical meaning of both narrations, you would see that although the methods are different, the intention is one and the same.

**SOPHIA:** Not only does the Platonic fable show itself to be made for some wise significance, but the Hebrew history also, in this first union and subsequent division of man, denotes a desire to signify something about human nature other than the literal history; for I do not truly believe that man and woman were at any time otherwise than in two separate bodies, as they are...

**FI.** God made man and woman in a form that they could generate, but the proper end of man is not generating, but to find happiness in divine contemplation and in the paradise of God. In doing this, they remained immortal and had no need for generation, because the human essence and species were preserved in them perpetually; and the immortal have no need for the generation of children of their species. See the angels, the planets, stars, and heavens, which do not generate children of their species. Generation, as *Aristotle* says <note>Aristotle argues in *On the Soul* (De Anima) and *On Generation and Corruption* that reproduction is the means by which mortal beings participate in the eternal and divine</note>, was as a remedy for mortality; and therefore man, so long as he was immortal, did not generate. But when he was already made mortal because of sin, he sought help through the generation of his like, to which God gave power so that, in one way or another, the human species would not perish.

God commanded Adam to eat of all these trees of paradise, and of the tree of life, because they would grant him eternal life; for the intellect becomes immortal and eternal through eternal cognitions—especially divine ones—and thus reaches its own proper happiness. But of the tree of the knowledge of good and evil he was not to eat, because it would make him mortal; that is, he should not become...

-> Aa 2 <-

...the intellect to the acts of sensuality, to corporeal exercise—such as sensual delights and the acquisition of useful things—which are good in appearance, but bad in essence. And these are also called the **tree of knowledge of good and evil**: because in the knowledge of them it is not appropriate to say "true" or "false," as is the case with intellectual and eternal things; rather, one can only say "good" or "bad," according to how they accommodate the appetite of man. For if one says that the Sun is larger than the earth, the response will not be that this is "good" or "bad," but that it is "true" or "false." But if one acquires riches, you will not say "true" or "false," but you will say "good" or "bad." <note>Philo distinguishes between speculative reason (seeking objective truth/falsehood) and practical or moral choice (seeking what is perceived as good or bad for the self).</note>

Following these corporeal cognitions—which divert the intellect from those things in which its own happiness consists—is the "tree of knowledge of good and evil" that was prohibited to **Adam**. For this alone could make him mortal: because just as true and eternal divine things make the intellect divine, true, and eternal like themselves, so sensual, corporeal, and corruptible things make it material and corruptible like themselves. <note>In the Platonic and Aristotelian tradition, the soul "becomes" what it contemplates; by focusing on the physical, the soul loses its divine, eternal quality.</note>

Yet the Divinity, foreknowing that this way of union between the two parts of man—and the obedience of the feminine corporeal part to the masculine intellectual part—though it made man happy and rendered his essence (which is his intellectual soul) immortal, it would cause his corporeal and feminine part to decay more quickly. This occurs both in the individual—for when the intellect is inflamed in the cognition and love of eternal and divine things, it abandons the care of the body and lets it perish before its time—and also in the succession of the <term>human species</term>. <note>Philo argues that intense intellectual life can lead to the neglect of health and the cessation of reproduction, as the philosopher ignores physical needs.</note> This is because those who are ardent for intellectual contemplations despise corporeal loves and flee the

# DIALOGO

<page-num>38</page-num>

This is what the text means when it says, "it is not good for man to be alone; let us make him a helper in front of, or against him": <note>original: "facciamgli adiutorio in front ouero contra di lui." Whereupon, after He showed him all the animals and man recognized in all of them how each inclined toward bodily sustenance and the generation of their own kind, man began to find himself deficient, because he did not yet possess a similar cause or inclination toward the physical feminine part; and he desired to imitate the animals in this regard. Then, as the text says, God allowed a deep sleep to take hold of Adam, and while he slept, He divided the feminine part from the masculine, which man from then on recognized as a wife separate from himself. This means that as sleep came upon him—which is a deprivation and a rest from that initial intellectual wakefulness and that ardent contemplation—the intellect began to incline toward the physical part, as a husband to a wife, and to take a tempered care for its sustenance as if it were his own part, and for the procreation of his like for the preservation of the species. Thus, the division between the masculine and feminine mediums was for a good purpose.

These two halves are not "infused intellect" and "innate talent" (as some imagine), but rather the masculine intellectual part and the feminine corporeal part, which together make the whole man. For if man were entirely speculative, he would have belonged to the genus of the angels and spiritual beings, which was outside the intention of the Creator; His intent was that he should be a man with an alternation between intellect and body. If man converted entirely into something angelic, it would destroy the human composition, the preservation of the individual, and the succession of the species. 

And this is his "struggle against the gods" that Plato describes. Hence, he had them divided; that is, he caused the body to offer some resistance to the intellect, and the intellect to incline toward the necessary cares and natural functions of the body, so that life would be human rather than angelic. He says that from this division, Love <term>amore</term> was born, because every half desires and loves the reintegration <term>redintegratione</term> <note>The act of making something whole again; restoration to a perfect state.</note> of its remaining half. In effect, the intellect would never care for the body if it were not for the love it has for its feminine corporeal partner; nor would the body be governed by the intellect, if not for the love and affection it has for its masculine partner. # DIALOGO #

[Plato writes that the two halves] did not seek the things necessary for their sustenance and were perishing; therefore, as a remedy, Jupiter <note>original: "Iuppiter"; the Roman name for the king of the gods, used here to represent the Creator within the classical framework of the myth.</note> had their genitals turned <note>original: "to re"; likely *volgere* (to turn) or *porre* (to place), referring to the mythic repositioning of human anatomy to allow for frontal reproduction.</note> toward one another. Once sexual intercourse <term>coito</term> and the generation of their like were satisfied, the division was reintegrated. This signifies that the purpose of their division into an intellectual part and a corporeal part was so that by taking satisfaction in physical delights, they might sustain themselves as individuals and generate their like for the perpetual conservation of the species. 

It then warns that one must not sin, because every "half" of the man would then come to be divided again, and each would remain only a "quarter" of a man. This means that if the intellectual part is not united, but rather divided from perfect knowledge <term>cognitioni</term> and wise counsel, it remains imperfect and unstable by nature; for unity is what makes it vigorous and perfect, and division robs it of its perfection and vigor. 

And likewise, the corporeal part is perfect when it is united in seeking what is necessary; but when it is divided by the acquisition of superfluous and insatiable things, it remains imperfect and fragile. In such a way, through this division of each of the parts, man fails not only in that first intellectual union of the Androgyne <note>A mythical primordial human being who combined male and female traits, symbolizing a state of original wholeness.</note>, but even in being that "half" which human life requires; instead, he remains a "half of a half," following a lascivious and sinful life. This is what the Platonic fable <note>Specifically, the myth of the halves related by Aristophanes in Plato's *Symposium*.</note> signifies allegorically; and the specific details he writes regarding the manner of dividing, consulting, and such, are ornaments of the fable to make it more beautiful and plausible.

...[suc]cess, O Philo, with the interpretation of that allegory for our purpose regarding the birth of love.

**Filone:** The interpretation we derive from this allegory for our purpose regarding the birth of love is that all human loves and desires are born from the reciprocal division of the intellect and the human body. For the intellect, being inclined toward its body—as the male is toward the female—desires and loves the things pertaining to it; and if these are necessary and moderate, they are virtuous <term>onesti</term> <note>original: "honeşti"; refers to desires that are morally upright and balanced.</note> desires and loves, owing to their moderation and temperament. But if they are superfluous, they are lascivious and dishonest inclinations and sinful acts. 

Furthermore, the body, loving the intellect as a woman loves her male husband, rises up to desire its perfections, soliciting through the senses—with the eyes, ears, and feeling—as well as the imagination <term>fantasia</term>, and memory, to acquire what is necessary for right knowledge <term>cognitioni</term> and eternal intellectual habits <term>habiti</term> <note>original: "habiti"; in the Aristotelian sense, these are stable dispositions or qualities of the mind acquired through practice.</note>. Through these, the human intellect attains its happiness <note>original: "si felicita"; literally "makes itself happy" or "reaches beatitude".</note>. These are absolutely virtuous desires and loves; and the more ardent they are, the more laudable and perfect they become. 

Thus, in this way, Plato has shown the birth of love, and specifically of all human loves, for which he makes the intellectual part the father and the corporeal part the mother. And the first love of man is this mutual, individual one between one part and the other, like the love that exists between the male and the female. After this firstborn love, all human desires and loves for all things are born from these two parents. These are included in three species: namely, the intellectual ones, which are absolutely virtuous, such as were those of man when he was joined and whole in his first happy life in paradise.

[Pe]nia, <note>The text begins mid-word, completing "Penia," the personification of Poverty.</note> forced by necessity, thought of a way she might become pregnant by some trick with a son of Porus <note>Poro or Porus represents "Plenty" or "Resourcefulness."</note>; thus she went to lie down beside him, and from him conceived Love. He always has a desire for beautiful things because Venus herself is beautiful. Because he is the son of the god Porus and the poor woman Penia, he shares in the nature of both.

On the one hand, he is dry and squalid, with bare feet, always flying along the ground, without a house or a shelter, without a bed or any covering; he sleeps in the streets in the open air, preserving the nature of his mother, who is always in need. On the other hand, following his father’s lineage, he pursues beautiful and good things. He is high-spirited and bold, a powerful and clever hunter, always plotting new schemes, a student of prudence, eloquent, and throughout his life a philosopher—and also a deceiver, an enchanter, a sorcerer <note>original: "venefico"; literally one who uses potions or spells.</note>, and a sophist.

According to his mixed nature, he is neither entirely immortal nor mortal; rather, in the short space of a single day he dies and lives. If he is revived once, he fails another time, and he does this many times because of the mixture of his father’s and mother’s natures. Whatever he acquires, he loses, and what he loses, he recovers; for this reason, he is never a beggar, yet never rich. He is also situated between wisdom <term>sapientia</term> and ignorance <term>ignorantia</term>. This is because none of the gods practice philosophy, nor do they desire to become wise, because they already are wise. In effect, no wise person practices philosophy. Nor do those who are entirely ignorant practice it, for they never desire to be wise. Truly, this is the worst trait of the ignorant person: that he is not wise, yet does not desire to be so, because he never desires the things he does not know he lacks. ...at the birth of *Venus*, *Penia* <note>Penia; representing Poverty or Lack.</note>, being in need, stood outside to gather some scraps of the gods' food; and the god *Porus* <note>Porus; representing Resource, Plenty, or Wealth.</note>, son of Counsel, drunk on nectar, left the house where he had been feasting with the others and went into the garden to sleep. This means that when the gods—that is, God, together with the angelic world—produced beauty similar to their own within the created corporeal world, where they joined together in liberal generosity and joy, as if at a birthday feast, the deficiency of potential matter <term>materia potentiale</term> <note>In Aristotelian philosophy, "potential matter" is the raw substance of the universe that has the potential to take on any form but possesses none of its own.</note> intervened there, longing to share in the beautiful forms and the divine and angelic perfections. *Porus*, the son of Counsel—representing the influential Intellect—being "drunk with nectar"—meaning full of Divine Ideas and forms—desired to share these with the lower world to bring it to goodness; even though inclining toward what is below was a kind of lack for him. And this is what is meant when it is said that he went to sleep in the garden of Jupiter <note>original: "Gioue"</note>: that is, he lulled his vigilant cognition to sleep, directing it toward the corporeal world of motion and generation, which is the "garden of Jupiter." For the celestial Intellect is the house and palace of Jupiter, where the banquet is held and the divine nectar is drunk—this nectar being the eternal contemplation and the desire for the divine and most beautiful Majesty. When the Intellect, the son of Counsel (who is the supreme God), wished to share himself with the lower world, the poor and needy *Penia* approached him—that is, the poverty of matter, longing for perfection. She became pregnant by him while he was "drunk" with the desire for corporeal perfection and half-asleep to his eternal divine contemplation, having turned away from it somewhat to share perfection...

-> # D I A L O G O <-

...and to the needy matter, and from both of them Love was born; because Love signifies perfection not in act <term>in atto</term> <note>In Aristotelian philosophy, "in act" or "actuality" refers to something that is fully realized or currently happening, as opposed to just having the potential to happen.</note>, but in potential <term>in potentia</term> <note>"In potential" or "potentiality" refers to the capacity for something to become something else or to acquire a quality it does not yet have.</note>. And such is the intellect within the generable body, which is a potential form and a **possible intellect** <note>The "possible intellect" (intelletto possibile) is a philosophical term for the human mind's capacity to receive and process information, which is "empty" until it learns.</note>; because it is an intellect, it knows beautiful things, but because it exists in potential, it lacks the possession of them and desires actual beauty. This is why it is said that Love is a middle point between the beautiful and the ugly; for the possible intellect and material forms are halfway between pure matter—which is entirely without form—and the separate forms and actual angelic intelligences, which are truly beautiful. 

Therefore, Diotima assigns equally to Love the conditions and contrivances of needy, mortal, variable, and imperfect corporeal matter—his mother—and the intellectual and perfect conditions of the affluent intellect, *Porus* <note>Porus represents Resource or Plenty.</note>, his father. And she portrays him as a **philosopher** <note>Literally a "lover of wisdom" (from the Greek 'philo-' and 'sophia').</note> and not "wise"; for the possible intellect desires wisdom and exists in the potential for it, as it is not wise in act, like the angelic intellect. 

Nor did Diotima fail to show in this fable of hers that the possible intellect participates in the **agent intellect** <term>intelletto agente</term> <note>The "agent" or "active" intellect was thought to be the divine or higher power that "shines a light" on the human mind, allowing it to turn potential thoughts into actual knowledge.</note>, or in the angelic or divine act, and that its potentiality does not come from its own intellectual nature, as some believe, but only from its association with needy matter, which is deprived of all actuality and is pure potentiality. She also taught that the first producer of generated Love is generated beauty, and its true parents are the knowledge of beauty—which is the father—and the lack of beauty—which is the mother; for whatever is loved and desired must be previously known as beautiful, and it must be lacking, or able to be lacked, so that one desires to preserve it forever.

-> ### THIRD BOOK ### <-

...that you, oh **Sofia**, recognize that the father of universal love in the lower world is the knowledge of beauty, and the mother is **lack** <term>mancamento</term> <note>In this context, 'lack' or 'deficiency' refers to the state of being without something desired; it is the philosophical equivalent of the Greek *Penia* (Poverty).</note>.

**Sofia**: I understand this, but these parents seem to me to apply only to the corporeal world, and even then only to the lower realm of things that are born and perish. Yet I have already heard from you that love is found first and primarily in the angelic world. Do you assign these same two specific causes—namely, the knowledge of beauty and the lack of it—to that world as well?

**Filone**: It is true that love exists not only in the lower worlds, but primarily in the angelic world through the knowledge of a beauty that is lacked. However, this is that immense and divine beauty which all created intellects lack, and which they know, love, and desire. Plato calls this beauty **Great Venus** <note>original: "magna venere"</note>, which represents the beauty of the intellectual world. This beauty was not born in time, for it is eternal and immutable, nor does the love for it have "new births." If it can be said to have been born at all, it was born from eternity in that divine world. 

Furthermore, the "lack" in that realm does not arise from the company of needy **Penia** (meaning matter) with the intellect, because no matter is found in that world. Instead, the lack arises from the very condition of the creature: by the mere fact of being created, it lacks the supreme perfection of its Creator, whose excellence of beauty stands far above that of the creature. Therefore, these specific "parents" [Plenty and Poverty] are proper to the love generated in the lower world, at the birth of the **Lower Venus**—that is, the beauty distributed among physical bodies. This is not the same as the love of the angelic world, which is superior even to **Porus** <note>The personification of Resource or Plenty.</note> embraced in the garden of **Jove** <note>Jupiter or Zeus.</note>, and is entirely alien to needy Poverty.

**Sofia**: I have understood from you what the poets and philosophers have fabled regarding the birth...

# DIALOGO #

...ment <note>original: "mẽto", likely the conclusion of a word like *nascimento* (birth) or *fondamento* (foundation)</note> of love, and its progenitors, and what their fables wisely signify. **FI.** <note>Filone</note>: I will first tell you, oh **Sofia**, those whom I believe to be in common the father and mother of every love; and then, if you wish, I will apply them to human love and to the worldly love as well.

**SO.** <note>Sofia</note>: I like this order, because common knowledge should be placed before the more particular. Tell me, then, who is the common father of every love, and who is its mother?

**FI.**: I do not make the mother pure **lack** <term>carentia</term> <note>From the Latin *carentia*, meaning the state of being without or wanting something.</note>, as **Diotima** <note>The wise woman in Plato’s *Symposium* who describes the birth of Love from Plenty and Poverty.</note> does, nor the father affluent knowledge, as she wishes. But leaving aside the fictions and opinions of others, I tell you that the common father of every love is **the beautiful**, and the common mother is the **knowledge of the beautiful mixed with lack**. From these two, as from a true father and mother, love and desire are generated; because the beautiful, known by one who lacks it, is immediately loved and desired by the knowing lover who longs for that beauty. And thus is born love, conceived by the beautiful in the mind of its knower, who lacks it and desires it. Therefore, the beautiful that is loved is the father and generator of love, and the mother is the **mind of the lover** impregnated by the seed of that beauty—which is its exemplary beauty within the mind of the knower. Being thus impregnated, the mind desires union...

The contradiction is this: if the mind of the knower is pregnant with beauty, she does not lack it—rather, she possesses it, because a pregnant woman has the child within her and does not lack it.

**FI.** <note>Filone</note>: If the form of beauty were not in the mind of the lover under the guise of the beautiful, the good, and the pleasant, that beauty would never be loved by him. Those who are entirely deprived of beauty neither possess nor desire the beautiful; but the one who does desire it is not entirely deprived of it, because he possesses the knowledge of it, and his mind is impregnated with the form of its beauty. However, because he lacks the principal thing—which is **perfect union** with that beauty—he feels the desire for the principal effect that is missing, and he desires to enjoy the beautiful through union. The form of beauty imprinted in his mind incites him, just as a pregnant woman desires to give birth and bring to light that which is hidden within her. So, even though the mother of love (that is, the lover) is deprived of perfect union with the beloved, she is not deprived of the **exemplary form** <term>forma essemplare</term> <note>In Renaissance Neo-Platonism, this refers to the ideal mental blueprint or "idea" of a thing that exists in the mind before the thing itself is fully realized or possessed.</note> of its beauty. It is this form that makes her a lover, desiring union with the beauty that she lacks.

**SO.**: I like what you say, but there remains for me...

**Filone**: This definition of beauty given by some modern philosophers is not really appropriate, nor perfect; for if it were so, no simple body—not composed of diverse and proportioned parts—would be called beautiful. Therefore, the Sun, the Moon, and the Stars would not be beautiful, nor would radiant **Venus**, nor illustrious **Jupiter**.

**Sofia**: Yet these also possess the beauty of the circular figure, which is the most beautiful of all shapes, which is a whole in itself and contains parts.

**Filone**: The circular figure is indeed beautiful in itself, but its beauty is not the proportion of parts to one another, nor to the whole, because its parts are equal and homogeneous <term>homogeneous|consisting of parts all of the same kind; uniform</term>, in which no proportion can exist. Nor is the beauty of the circular shape what makes the Sun, Moon, and Stars beautiful; if that were the case, every spherical body would have the beauty of the Sun. Rather, their beauty is luminosity <note>original: "lucidità"</note>, which in itself is not a shape, nor does it have proportioned parts. Likewise, flaming fire, gleaming gold, and bright, precious gems would not be beautiful, because all these are simple <term>simple|in classical philosophy, "simple" means made of one single substance rather than a mixture of elements</term>, and the parts and the whole are of one nature, without any proportional diversity. Furthermore, according to those philosophers, only the whole would be beautiful, and none of the parts would be beautiful except in comparison to the whole. Again, you will sometimes see a face be beautiful at one time and not at another, even though the proportion of its parts to the whole remains exactly the same. It appears, then, that beauty does not lie in the proportions of parts. And besides that, if their view were true, lovely colors would not be beautiful, nor would light—which is the most beautiful thing in the corporeal world—and

You will well realize, O Sofia, how much more beautiful the **Idea** of the craftwork must be when it is united in the mind of the craftsman than when it is found distributed and dismembered within a physical body; for union increases every beauty and perfection, while division diminishes it.

The parts of the beauty of a statue of **Venus** in wood are divided, each one on its own, which makes its beauty slow and weak compared to that which is in the soul of the craftsman; for in the soul consists the **Idea of the art** with all its parts **complicated** <term>complicated|From the Latin "complicare," meaning "folded together." In this philosophical sense, it describes many parts existing as a single, unified whole before they are "unfolded" into the physical world.</term> together, in such a way that one favors the other and makes it grow in beauty. The beauty of the whole exists in each part, and the beauty of each part exists in the whole without any division or discrepancy. In this way, anyone who could see both would recognize that the art is, without comparison, more beautiful than the crafted object, as the art is the cause of the crafted beauty—which, in the company of physical bodies, loses as much of its perfection as the bodies gain from it.

For the more a coarse and ugly body is drawn toward the **form**, the more beautiful the crafted object becomes; and the more the form is pulled down and hindered by the body, the less beautiful the finished craftwork remains. It follows, then, that **form** without a body is most beautiful, just as a body without form is most ugly.

For if these [senses] were the knowers and lovers of beauty, it would follow that everyone would equally know the beauties of physical things, and equally delight in them and love them, because everyone has eyes and ears. Yet you will see many beautiful things that are not recognized by many "clear eyes," <note>The speaker suggests that having physically healthy vision does not guarantee the ability to perceive aesthetic or spiritual beauty.</note> nor do they offer delight or love to those who see them; and how many men with good hearing will you see who have no taste for **music** <term>musica: here referring not just to sound, but to the mathematical and cosmic harmony it represents</term>, nor does it seem beautiful to them, nor do they love it; and others to whom beautiful verses and orations seem useless. It seems, then, that the knowledge of physical beauties, and the delight and love of them, does not consist in the eyes and ears through which they pass, but in the soul where they go.

**SO.** Even though in this you favor my doubt, I will interrupt your answer until you tell me the reason why all souls do not equally have **knowledge** <note>original: "cognitione"</note>, delight, and love of the beautiful...

**FI.** You will see the answer to this, together with the solution to your doubt, if you will let me speak. You know that corporeal beauties are formal graces; and I have already told you that all abstract forms, in a connective order, are found spiritually in the World Soul <note>The "World Soul" (*Anima Mundi*) is a Neoplatonic concept of a cosmic spirit that bridges the gap between the divine intellect and the material world.</note>, of which our rational soul is an image. This is because its essence is a latent configuration of all those spiritual forms, through the impression made upon it by the World Soul, which is its exemplary origin. This latent configuration is what Aristotle calls *potentiality* <note>original: *potentia*</note> and *universal preparation* in the intellect, which is capable of receiving and understanding all forms and essences. For if they were not all within the soul in a potential or latent way, it could not receive them and understand each one of them in act and through pre-existence. 

Plato says that our reasoning and understanding is a reminiscence <note>original: *reminiscentia*; Plato’s theory that learning is actually a process of "remembering" knowledge the soul possessed before birth.</note> of things previously existing in the soul, in a state of oblivion; this is the same as the *potentiality* of Aristotle and the "latent way" of which I speak to you. Thus, you will recognize that all forms and species do not "jump" from physical bodies into our soul—because for something to migrate from one subject to another is impossible. Instead, when they are represented through the senses, they cause those same forms and essences to shine forth, which were already luminous within our soul. 

Aristotle calls this shining forth the "act of understanding," and Plato calls it "recollection"; but their intention is one and the same, despite their different ways of speaking. Our soul is, therefore, full of formal beauties; indeed, these are its own essence. And if they are hidden within it, this latency does not arise from the intellect itself (which makes beauty essential to the soul), but from the faculty of cognition and the union that...

### T H I R D.

...[ought to] flee and hate: and what the perfect knowledge and love of those things is, and what is the false, sophisticated, and apparent. You have understood that the soul is the intermediary between the intellect and the body—not only the soul of the world, but also our own, which is an image <note>original: *simulacro*; an image, likeness, or representation</note> of it. Therefore, our soul has two faces, just as I told you regarding the Moon between the Sun and the Earth: one face directed toward its superior intellect, and the other face toward the body, which is inferior to it. 

The first face, directed toward the intellect, is the intellectual faculty <term>intellectual faculty: the power of the soul to reason and understand universal truths</term>, through which it reasons with universal and spiritual knowledge, extracting the intellectual forms and essences from particular and sensible bodies, always converting the corporeal mode into the intellectual. 

The second face, which is directed toward the body, is the sense <note>original: *senso*; sensory perception</note>, which is the particular knowledge of corporeal things, joined with and mixed into the materiality of the corporeal things being known. These two faces have contrary or opposite motions: and just as our soul, with its first face or rational knowledge, makes the corporeal into the incorporeal, so with the second face or sensible knowledge—by approaching the sensed bodies and mixing with them—it contracts the incorporeal into the corporeal. 

Corporeal beauties are known by our soul through these two modes of knowledge, with both faces—that is, sensitively and bodily, or rationally and intellectually. And according to each of these two modes of knowing corporeal beauty, love for them is caused in the soul: that is, through sensible knowledge comes sensual love, and through rational knowledge comes spiritual love. There are many whose face of the soul toward bodies is luminous, while the other toward the intellect is dark; and this

...knowledge of beauty, and leaving behind the corporeal aspect of the sensible as something ugly, a mere husk of the incorporeal, or its shadow and image. They love sensible beauties only to the extent that their knowledge of them leads them to know and love the spiritual beauties found within the sensible. These spiritual beauties they love as the only true beauties, delighting in their enjoyment. 

As for the rest of corporeality and sensuality, they not only feel no love or delight for it, but they hate it as something ugly and material. They flee from it as from a harmful opposite, because the mixture of corporeal things hinders the happiness of our soul. This mixture deprives the "upper face" of its intellectual light by clouding it with the sensual light of the "lower face." <note>The author uses the Neoplatonic metaphor of the soul having two "faces": the lower face interacts with the physical world through the senses, while the upper face perceives divine and intellectual truths. Just as gold, when it is mixed with alloys, crude metals, and terrestrial parts, cannot be beautiful, perfect, or pure—because its goodness consists in being purified of every alloy and clear of every crude mixture—so the soul, when mixed with the love of sensual beauties, cannot be beautiful or pure, nor can it reach its beatitude, until it is purified and cleansed of the incitements of sensible beauties. Only then does it come to possess its own intellectual light without any hindrance, which is happiness itself.

I clearly see that corporeal beauties, insofar as they are beauties, are not actually corporeal, but are the sole **participation** <term>participation (participatione): a Platonic concept where physical things "take part in" or reflect higher, perfect spiritual realities</term> that corporeal things have with the incorporeal—or rather, the luster that spiritual things infuse into inferior bodies. Their beauties are truly shadows and images of incorporeal intellectual beauties. I see that the good of our soul is to ascend from corporeal beauties into spiritual ones, and to know the superior intellectual beauties through the inferior sensible ones. 

But with all this, I still have a desire to know what this **spiritual beauty** <term>spiritual beauty: the inner, essential beauty of the soul or divine forms, as opposed to outward physical appearance</term> is, which makes every incorporeal thing beautiful, and which also communicates itself to bodies—and not only to the celestial bodies in a great way, but even to the inferior and corruptible ones, according to whether they participate more or less; and most of all to man, and principally to his **rational soul** <term>rational soul (anima rationale): the part of the human soul capable of reason and logic, distinguishing humans from animals</term> and **intellectual mind** <term>intellectual mind (mente intellettiua): the highest faculty of the soul, capable of direct spiritual intuition</term>. 

What then is this beauty that is thus spread throughout the entire universe and in each of its parts? And through which all beautiful things, and each of them, is made beautiful? For though you have declared to me that beauty is **formal grace** <term>formal grace (gratia formale): a beauty arising from the "form" or design given by God, rather than the raw material itself</term>, the knowledge of which moves us to love, this only describes the beauty of formed bodies and their physical shapes. I would like to know how this is a shadow and image of the incorporeal...

## DIALOGUE

<note>Sofia is speaking</note>
...to know precisely what this incorporeal beauty is, upon which corporeal beauty depends. For when I know this, I shall recognize what true beauty is—that which is distributed among all things—and I will have no need for a particular knowledge or definition of the corporeal beauty you have given me. Indeed, the definition of the corporeal is not a definition of beauty itself, but rather of beauty as it exists within a body. If I know what that same beauty is in its own essence, I will understand it as it relates to bodies; and this is what I principally desire to know. I pray you, along with the other things, that you might also show me this.

**FI.** Just as with beautiful artifacts <note>Objects created by human skill or artifice.</note>, as you have already understood, beauty is nothing other than the art of the craftsman <term>craftsman (artefice): in this context, the artisan or the divine creator who shapes matter according to a mental plan</term> anticipated and then diffused within those crafted bodies and their parts. Thus, the true and primary artificial beauty is the scientific art <term>scientific art (scientifica arte): knowledge or skill based on certain principles, existing in the mind before it is applied to matter</term> pre-existing in the mind of the craftsman, upon which the beauties of the crafted bodies depend, as if communicated to all of them from their primary Idea. In the same way, the beauty of all natural bodies is nothing else than the splendor of their Ideas; wherefore these Ideas are the true beauties, through which all bodies are beautiful.

**SO.** You are explaining the matter to me using something that is no less hidden than the thing itself. You tell me that the true beauties are the Ideas, but I have no less need for you to explain to me what an "Idea" is than what "beauty" is. This is especially true since the existence of Ideas, as you know, is much more hidden from us than the existence of beauty itself. You wish, then, to explain the more manifest by the more obscure. Furthermore, not only is the existence of the Idea more occult than that of beauty, it is also much more doubtful and uncertain; for while everyone concedes that there is a true beauty from which all others depend, many of the wisest philosophers <note>The text cuts off here; Sofia is likely about to mention philosophers who doubt the existence of Platonic Ideas, such as Aristotle.</note>

# TEORIZZO

Dd 2

...[they] deny the existence of Platonic Ideas, as does Aristotle and all his Peripatetic <note>Followers of Aristotle, known for his empirical approach as opposed to Plato's idealism.</note> followers. How then do you wish to clarify for me the certain by the doubtful, and the more manifest by the hidden?

**FI.** Ideas are nothing other than the conceptions of the created universe with all its parts pre-existing in the intellect of the **supreme Artificer** <term>supreme Artificer (sommo opifice): a term for God as the ultimate architect or craftsman who designed the universe</term> and creator of the world; their existence no subject of reason can deny.

This [order] is not only most marvelous in the whole, but even in the very smallest of its parts it is a cause of great admiration to every wise person who considers it. In the order and correspondence of each of those smallest parts, one sees the supreme perfection of the mind of the Artificer of the world and the infinite wisdom of its creator.

**SO.** This I would certainly not deny, nor do I believe it can be denied; for in myself and in each of my limbs I see the great wisdom of the creator of all things, which surpasses my own understanding and that of every wise man.

**FI.** You understand well; especially if you were to see the **anatomy** of the human body and each of its parts—with what subtlety of art and wisdom it is composed and formed—for in each of those parts would be presented to you the immense wisdom, providence, and care of God our creator. ### THEORY

...something of the difference that exists between them regarding the being of **Ideas**, which both *Aristotle* and his followers strove so hard to deny.

**FI.** I will tell you. In short, know that *Plato* placed within the **Ideas** all existence and the substance of things. In this way, everything created within the corporeal world is considered to be more a shadow of substance and essence than something that can truly be called essence or substance itself. Thus, he disregards corporeal beauties in themselves, for he says that they exist for no other reason than to show themselves to us and lead us to the knowledge of those higher Ideas; in themselves, their beauty is little more than nothing.

*Aristotle* wishes to be more temperate in this matter, for it seems to him that the supreme perfection of the **artificer** <note>The "Artificer" or "Demiurge" refers to the divine creator.</note> ought to produce works that are perfect in themselves. Therefore, he maintains that within the corporeal world and its parts resides the essence and the proper substance of each one of them. He holds that **Ideal knowledge** <term>Ideal knowledge: the blueprints or "Forms" in the divine mind.</term> is not the essence and substance of things, but rather their productive and ordering causes. 

For this reason, he maintains that the **primary substances** <term>primary substances (prime sustātie): In Aristotelian logic, these are individual, specific things (like a specific person or a specific tree) rather than general categories.</term> are individuals, and that within each of them, the essence of the **species** is preserved. Regarding these species, he does not want the **universals** to be the Ideas (which are the causes of real things), but rather merely intellectual concepts of our rational soul, taken from the substance and essence that exists in each of the real individuals. Therefore, he calls those universal concepts **secondary substances**, as they are abstracted by our intellect from the primary individuals. 

He does not want the Ideas to be "primary substances," as *Plato* says, nor even "secondary" ones, but rather the **primary causes** of all corporeal substances and of all their essences composed of **matter and form**. This is because he holds that matter and the body enter into the essence and substance of corporeal things, and that in the...

<meta>This page continues Filone’s explanation of the divergence between Plato and Aristotle. ->DIALOGO<-

...definition of every essence, and that this is done through **genus** and **difference** <term>genus and difference: A method of definition where a thing is first placed in a broad category (genus) and then distinguished by its specific characteristic (difference).</term>, matter—or corporeality, or a common material form—enters first as the **genus**, while the special form enters as the **difference**. Because essence and substance are constituted of both matter and form, and since in the **Ideas** there is neither matter nor body, Aristotle believes that neither "essence" nor "substance" can be strictly attributed to them. Instead, they are the divine principle upon which all essences and substances depend: that is, the former are primary corporeal effects, and the latter are their spiritual images. He maintains, therefore, that the beauties of the corporeal world are true beauties, but they are caused by and dependent upon the primary **Ideal beauties** of the first divine intellect. From this difference between these two theologians <note>original: "theologhi." In the Renaissance, "theologian" often referred to philosophers like Plato and Aristotle who studied the first causes and the divine.</note> arise all the others found between them regarding the **Ideas**, as well as the greater part of all their theological and natural disagreements.

**SO.** I am pleased to know this difference, and I would also like to know your opinion on which of them you most agree with in this matter.

**FI.** When you consider this difference well, you will find it lies more in the application of words than in their actual meaning—specifically, in the manner in which terms like essence, substance, unity, truth, goodness, beauty, and other similar ones should be used when describing the reality of things. Thus, in their actual judgment, I follow both of them, for their conclusion is one and the same. In the use of words, perhaps Aristotle is to be followed, because the "modern" <note>Though ancient to us, Aristotle was "modern" relative to Plato; Filone suggests Aristotle refined and systematized the philosophical vocabulary that Plato used more poetically.</note> refines the language more, and is accustomed to assigning words to things more distinctly and subtly. I will tell you this: Plato, finding that the first philosophers of Greece <note>A reference to the Pre-Socratic philosophers, who often focused on material elements like water, fire, or air.</note> did not value any essences, substances, or beauties other than corporeal ones, and outside of the corp—

<meta>This page continues Filone’s explanation of the historical and philosophical roles of Plato and Aristotle. # T E O R I Z I O.
<note>theoretical discourse</note>

...more than people thought they were nothing. It was necessary, like a true physician, to cure them with the opposite; showing them that bodies in themselves possess no **essence**, no **substance**, and no beauty, as is truly the case. For a body has nothing other than the shadow of that incorporeal, **Ideal essence** and beauty from the mind of the **supreme architect of the world** <term>supreme architect: A reference to the "Demiurge" or Creator who shapes the universe according to divine patterns.</term>. 

Aristotle, however, later found that philosophers—because of the doctrine of **Plato**—had become entirely removed from the study of bodies. They estimated that all beauty, **essence**, and **substance** resided only in the **Ideas**, and nothing in the corporeal world. Seeing this, he realized they were becoming negligent in the knowledge of physical things: their actions, motions, natural alterations, and the causes of their **generation and corruption** <term>generation and corruption: The Aristotelian terms for the birth/creation and death/decay of physical objects.</term>. From such negligence, a defect would eventually result in our abstract knowledge of spiritual principles; for a deep knowledge of **effects** <note>the physical world</note> ultimately leads to a perfect knowledge of their **causes** <note>the divine realm</note>. 

Therefore, it seemed to him the right time to temper this extreme, which perhaps in its progress would have overshot the **Platonic** middle ground. And he demonstrated, as I have told you, that there are properly produced **essences** and **substances** within the corporeal world caused by the **Ideas**, and that there are also true beauties within it, though they remain dependent upon the purest and most perfect **Ideals**. 

So it was that **Plato** was a physician who cured a disease of excess, while **Aristotle** was a physician who preserved the health already introduced by Plato’s work, through the use of moderation.

**SO.** I have received no small satisfaction in knowing what **Ideas** mean, how their existence is necessary, and that Aristotle does not absolutely deny them. I also understand the difference between him and Plato in how they understand and speak of them. I will ask you no more about this, so as not to divert you from our main purpose.

this Ideal emanation, the principle of all creations, he not only described under the form and name of supreme wisdom, but he also declared it under the form and name of beauty in his song <note>The "Cantica" or Song of Songs, traditionally attributed to King Solomon.</note>; hence, speaking of her, he says: *You are all beautiful, my companion, and there is no flaw in you.* <note>original: *Bella sei tutta compagna mia, e difetto non è in te*; see Song of Solomon 4:7.</note> See how clearly he denotes the supreme Ideal beauty of divine wisdom by placing beauty within her entire being, without the mixture of any defect. **FI.** Good and evil can exist within a single subject—not in the same way, but in different aspects. A thing may be good in some small, apparent part, but evil in its greater part, more deeply and essentially. Such are the evil and intemperate pleasures: insofar as they delight, they are and appear good, but in themselves they are evil. This is because the "good" they derive from their form <note>In the philosophical tradition of this period, "form" gives a thing its essence and beauty, while "matter" is the physical substance that can be corrupt or lacking.</note> is joined to the "sickness" of their matter and submerged within it. Thus, they are inherently evil, yet possess some appearance of good that delights. Furthermore, this is not an absolute good, nor even an apparent good to everyone; it is only so to those intemperate desirers who are drawn to a minimal good without considering the overwhelming evil beneath it. The temperate, however, are not deceived by that small, apparent good; they recognize the excessive evil with which it is mixed. Therefore, they do not judge it to be delightful or desirable, but rather a true pain <note>original: *vera doglia*.</note> which ought to be abhorred, feared, and fled. Many such examples are found in the carnal appetite <note>original: *appetito carnale*; physical or bodily cravings.</note>, for most pleasures of taste, of Venereal <note>original: *Venereo*; referring to physical intimacy or sexual touch, named after the goddess Venus.</note> touch, and other luxuries <note>original: *mollitie*; literally "softness," referring to a lifestyle of over-indulgence or decadence.</note> are evil and ruinous.

...tremely <note>The word begins mid-sentence from the previous page: "estremamente" (extremely).</note> delightful; and the lover desires to enjoy the delight of the honorable acquisition. **SO.** Then why does *Aristotle* call only one "the love of the delightful," and names the others differently?

**FI.** Because in common speech, carnal delights are called—and are properly considered to be—delights. Such things are more truly "desired" than "loved," as you have understood; and if they have some beauty, it is so overcome by the baseness of the matter that it is submerged in its own deformity, and their goodness [is lost] in the malice of that deformity. Hence, the good and the beautiful found in them is only apparent, and not truly existing. 

But *Aristotle*, following common opinion, gave it the title of "the delightful." Regarding "the useful," even though it does not fail to delight many, he calls it "useful" to distinguish it from the former; both because it possesses utility to a greater degree than delight, and mainly because its delight—being within the spiritual imagination—is not as materially sensed as carnal delight. And as for "the honorable," even though it is much more—and more truly—delightful than the other two, he calls it "honorable"; both for its honor and its own specific character, and because its delight—being in the spiritual mind—is not materially sensed like carnal delight. This [carnal delight], as I have told you, although it appears most obvious to the common folk and even to beasts, is in effect worth little or nothing in terms of actual goodness or beauty.

But the intellectual virtues are entirely honorable and possess nothing of the material; for they do not deal with physical acts or corporeal delights from which they might take any matter, but rather with eternal things separate from bodies, and with the Intelligences <note>In Renaissance philosophy, "Intelligences" refers to celestial or angelic beings that govern the spheres.</note>. Thus, they are all intellectual forms without the company of matter; they are pure and truly honorable in themselves, and not merely by participation <note>original: "per participatione." A Platonic concept where a physical thing is only "good" because it "participates" in or reflects the ideal Form of Goodness.</note> like the others. It is for this reason that Plato calls the love of these virtues "divine."

**SO.** And the other species of love—what does Plato call them?

**FI.** He divides the genres of love into three, as Aristotle does, but in a different manner: these are bestial love, human love, and divine love. He calls "bestial" the excessive love of corporeal things that is neither tempered by the honorable nor measured by right reason. This applies to excessive carnal delights as well as to greed, the avarice for the useful, and other ambitions of the imagination <note>original: "fantastiche ambitioni." This refers to the "phantasy" or the faculty of the mind that processes sensory images, often leading to delusions if not governed by reason.</note>. Because all of these lack the moderation and tempering of the human intellect, they remain the loves of an animal without intellect, and are truly bestial. 

And he calls "human love" that which concerns the moral virtues, which temper all the sensual and imaginative acts of man and moderate his delight. Because this love possesses corporeal matter but an intellectual and honorable form, he calls it

...perfection <note>original: "tione"; completing the word "perfettione" from the previous page.</note> is the end of that love which precedes it. And furthermore, within man himself, his faculties are similarly subordinated, the lower to the higher; that is, those of the vegetative soul to those of the **sensitive soul** <note>The faculty of perception and movement common to animals.</note>, and those of the sensitive soul to those of the **intellective soul** <note>The rational faculty unique to humans among earthly beings.</note>, which is the final and supreme faculty, not only of man, but of the entire lower world. 

And even within this intellective faculty, the intellectual acts are ordered from lower to higher, according to the order of the **intelligible things** <note>original: "intelligibili"; objects or truths that can be grasped by the mind rather than perceived by the senses.</note> which are their object—from the lower to the higher, and so on up to the supreme and final Intelligible. This [supreme Intelligible], just as it is the highest being and the ultimate end to which all are ordered, so too is the act of human and angelic intention of which He is the object; it is the highest intellective act of the human, celestial, and angelic mind, to which all others are ordered as their final end and perfection.

...**said** <note>original: "detto"</note>, that the love produced in the intellect is the *tendency* of the first intellectual stage, directed toward the intelligible beauty, into the final unitive stage, which is perfect; and the delight in it is nothing else than that same unitive intellection of that intelligible beauty.

For just as in a father, the **productive love** <note>original: "l'amore produttiuo"; the love that moves one to create or generate something</note> of a son is not yet love for that son (who does not yet exist), but rather is love of himself—it is the father who, for his own perfection, desires to be a father, producing a son in his own image and likeness—and then a second, different love for the already-produced son makes him nourish, raise, and lead him to his possible perfection; so too the productive love of God in the universe is not initially the love He has for the universe itself, but another love that comes before it. That is: the love of Himself, desiring to share His **supreme beauty** in the universe produced in His image and likeness. But I clearly see that the cause of this transformation from human to divine is rather the divinity of your wise mind <note>The text here uses the truncated "men" for *mente* (mind).</note> than my own very lowly beauty.

**FI.** <note>Filone, the personification of the Lover</note> I would wish that this deception of yours regarding me would rather consist in making you love me with your soul <note>Italian: *an[ima]*.</note> as such, as would be fitting if you believed it, rather than saying it to me with your tongue. And if you indeed do not believe it (as is just), you cannot deny that the Supreme Beauty, which is greater and more excellent than all others infinitely, is not drawn back from the love of a base <note>Italian: *ba[ssa]*.</note> and finite human mind; if that mind loves it, the Supreme Beauty returns that love and draws it back, through the love that the mind bears toward it, into its most happy <note>Italian: *feliciſſ[ima]*.</note> and unitive delight. But you, who among humans so closely resemble <note>Italian: *[so]migli*.</note> that Supreme Beauty, why then do you not wish to resemble it in this <insert>grateful</insert> amorous reciprocation?

**SO.** <note>Sofia, the personification of Wisdom</note> Nor do I believe I differ much from it in this; for <note>Italian: *però ch[é]*.</note> just as it does not draw the lover to any union other than the spiritual union of the mind, and for that reason returns the love, so I do not wish to deny that I love you, and desire the union <note>Italian: *un[ione]*.</note> of your mind—not of yours with mine, but of mine with yours, as with one more perfect. And do not doubt this, given my diligence in contemplating the concepts of your mind and in enjoying your wisdom, from which I receive the greatest delight. Regarding the other corporeal union <note>Italian: *un[ione] corporea*.</note> that lovers usually desire, I do not believe nor would I wish that any such desire be found in you or in me; for just as spiritual love is entirely full of goodness <note>Italian: *[be]ne*.</note> and beauty, and all its effects are fitting <note>Italian: *conueni[enti]*.</note>...

<summary>Sofia and Filone discuss the "unitive" power of love, comparing the human intellectual love for beauty to the way the Supreme Beauty (God) draws the human mind toward itself. Sofia expresses a desire for a purely spiritual and intellectual union rather than a corporeal one.</summary>
<keywords>spiritual union, Supreme Beauty, Neoplatonism, intellectual love, reciprocation, Filone, Sofia</keywords>

### THIRD DIALOGUE ###

**246**

<meta>The body text is printed in an italic typeface. There is a pencil notation 'b' in the bottom right corner of the page margin.</meta>

*& health-giving, so I believe that corporeal love is rather evil and deformed, and its effects for the most part troublesome and harmful. And so that you may better answer me regarding this, tell me, I pray (as you have already promised me), about the effects of human love: which are good and praiseworthy, and which are pernicious and blameworthy, and which of these are more numerous? For with this final piece, you will have fulfilled all the obligations you incurred through your promises to me.*

**FI.** <note>Filone, whose name means "Lover" in Greek</note> *I see, O Sofia <note>Sofia's name means "Wisdom" in Greek</note>, that to escape my just accusations you demand payment on the remainder of my obligation. I recall giving you an ambiguous promise regarding that matter; and as you can well see, now is not the time to pay, for we have lingered long in this discussion on the origin of love, and it is already time to let you rest. Think instead of paying the debts you owe me, to which love, reason, and virtue <term>virtù: in the Renaissance sense, this refers to moral excellence and intellectual power</term> bind you; as for me, if I can find the time, I shall not fail to pay you that which my promise and my loving service toward you require of me.*

->*Farewell.* <note>original: "Vale," a standard Latin closing</note><-

<summary>Sofia asks Filone to categorize the effects of human love as good or bad to fulfill his intellectual debt to her; Filone postpones the discussion, noting the lateness of the hour, and closes the dialogue with a reminder of Sofia's own obligations to him.</summary>
<keywords>Leone Ebreo, Filone, Sofia, human love, moral obligation, virtue, Renaissance philosophy, conclusion</keywords>
